lines: I have a home warranty. Shouldn't they be paying for this?
I'm already paying for a home warranty. I'm not paying for this twice.
Why can't I just call my warranty company? Isn't that what it's for?
My warranty's supposed to cover all of this. Why would I pay you too?
followUps: So what am I paying them for, then?
Can't you just bill them directly?
delivery.speaker: primary

resolution.concern: She is afraid of paying twice for something she believes she already paid for, and of feeling foolish if the warranty does not cover it.
resolvedBy: Taking the warranty seriously and offering to help her check it
Being honest that coverage depends on her contract, without guessing
Explaining plainly what warranties often leave out, such as a service fee, permits, and code parts, and checking her contract for each
Explaining how a maintenance plan differs from a warranty if that comes up
Making it easy to call the warranty company first

evaluate.pass: The tech takes the warranty seriously, offers to check her contract or call with her, and explains plainly what it may not cover without guessing.
evaluate.fail: The tech says home warranties are worthless, guesses at what her contract covers, or pushes her to pay before she can check.

coaching.why: She believes she already paid for this, so a bill feels like paying twice. Mocking the warranty makes her defend it, and guessing at her coverage is a bluff. Helping her check, and explaining calmly what warranties often leave out, gets her a real answer either way.
coaching.modelResponse: Then let's use it if it covers this. I don't want you paying twice. Do you have the contract handy? Many warranties send their own company, charge a service fee, and leave out things like permits and code parts, but yours might not. If you call them first, I'll write down exactly what I found so they have it.
commonMistakes: Saying home warranties are a scam or a waste
Guessing what her contract covers without reading it
Pushing her to pay now instead of letting her call the warranty company
Pitching the membership before her warranty question is answered

review.author: Claude
notes: Written for linda-warranty. Fires at price (priceStated) per the assignment, though it sits in the membership group.
Claims about warranties are worded as "many" or "often" (service fee, permits, and code parts left out). Check against common California home warranty contracts before approval.

moves.name: How do I know it's really broken?
moves.summary: The customer asks how they can know the problem is real, since they cannot see it or check it themselves.

delivery.intent: Ask how you are supposed to know it is really broken, since you cannot see inside it and you are not a plumber. You are not accusing, but you are not taking their word for it either. Relax only when the tech shows you something you can see or check (the part, the leak, a photo, a reading) and explains it in plain words. If the tech just repeats that it is broken, press harder.
lines: How do I know it's actually broken? I can't see inside it.
No offense, but I just have to take your word for that?
It was working fine last week. How do I know that's the problem?
Can you show me? I'm not a plumber, I don't know what I'm looking at.
followUps: Okay, but how do I know that's not normal?
That's what you're telling me, though. Can I see it?
delivery.speaker: primary

resolution.concern: They cannot check the diagnosis themselves and fear paying for a repair they do not need. They need proof they can see, explained in words they understand.
resolvedBy: Showing the evidence, such as the part, the leak, a photo or video, or a reading
Explaining in plain words what it means and how it compares to normal
Inviting them to look and ask questions
Being honest about anything that is uncertain

evaluate.pass: The tech shows or offers to show the evidence (the part, the leak, a photo, a reading), explains it in plain words, and invites questions.
evaluate.fail: The tech says "trust me," repeats that it is broken without showing anything, explains it in trade terms, or makes the customer feel foolish for asking.

coaching.why: The customer cannot see inside the pipe or the tank, so every diagnosis asks them to take your word for it. Showing them is faster than convincing them. A photo, the old part, or a reading they can see answers the question better than any explanation.
coaching.modelResponse: Good question. You shouldn't have to take my word for it. Come take a look. This is where it's failing, and here's what it should look like for comparison. I took photos too, so you can keep them or show anyone you want. Does that make sense? What else would help you feel sure about it?
commonMistakes: Saying "trust me, I do this every day"
Explaining with trade terms instead of showing
Taking the question as an insult
Claiming the evidence shows more than it does

review.author: Claude
notes: Pairs with the show-what-you-found drill. In voice-only sessions, offering to show counts as showed_evidence under its definition.
passIf requires showed_evidence plus one of the plain-language behaviors. Confirm the engine reads allBehaviors and anyBehaviors together that way.

moves.name: I'll do part of it myself
moves.summary: The customer offers to do part of the job, such as hauling away the old unit, buying the parts, or finishing the easy work, to bring the price down.

delivery.intent: Offer to do part of the job yourself to bring the price down, such as hauling away the old unit, buying the parts, or finishing the easy part. Sound practical. If you are handy, sound a little proud of it. If the tech refuses everything, get suspicious. If the tech agrees to the parts that make sense and explains the rest plainly, relax.
lines: What if I haul the old one away myself? That's got to save something.
Could you just do the main part? I can handle the rest.
I can pick up the parts myself. Just charge me for the labor.
If I do some of the easy stuff, how much does that take off?
followUps: So you won't let me do any of it? Seems convenient.
How hard can it be, really? It's just a couple of connections.
delivery.speaker: primary

resolution.concern: They want to lower the cost and feel capable. They suspect the price includes easy work they could do themselves.
resolvedBy: Agreeing to the parts that are safe and reasonable for a homeowner, and saying what that takes off
Explaining plainly why gas, venting, and permitted work stay with a licensed tech
Being honest about how customer-supplied parts affect the warranty
Respecting their skills instead of talking down

evaluate.pass: The tech agrees to the parts the customer can safely do, says what that takes off the price, and explains plainly which parts must stay with a licensed tech.
evaluate.fail: The tech refuses every part without a reason, talks down to the customer, or invents rules to keep the whole job.

coaching.why: Most customers who offer to help are trying to save money, not insult you. Saying yes to the reasonable parts shows the rest of your answer is honest. Be specific about the parts that are not reasonable: gas, venting, and anything the permit or warranty depends on.
coaching.modelResponse: Sure, some of this you can do. If you want to haul the old one to the dump yourself, I'll take the haul-away charge off. The gas line, the venting, and the install itself I need to do, because they're on the permit and the warranty depends on them. Want me to redo the quote that way?
commonMistakes: Refusing every part without explaining why
Talking down to a customer who says they are handy
Inventing a rule or warranty term to keep the whole job
Letting the customer do gas or permitted work to close the sale

review.author: Claude
notes: Triggers on priceStated with the objections phase added, since customers offer to do part of the work after hearing the price. This is a small change from the scope pattern.
Fits handy or price-focused personas best (devin-researcher, rick-landlord, paul-engineer, ruiz-couple). Consider movePreferences weights if it sounds out of character for others.
Company policies on customer-supplied parts differ. Company specs should supply the exact warranty wording.

moves.name: I'll just call when it breaks
moves.summary: The tech offers the membership and the customer says they would rather pay for repairs when something breaks.

delivery.intent: Say you would rather pay for repairs when something breaks than pay for a plan. Be easygoing and practical. You think the math favors waiting. Accept an answer with real numbers and no pressure. If the tech pushes or predicts a disaster, become more firm.
lines: I'll just call you when something breaks. That's worked fine so far.
Why pay for a plan when nothing's wrong? I'll pay when I need you.
I'd rather keep my money and call if there's a problem.
If something goes wrong, I've got your number. That's good enough for me.
followUps: Things don't break that often. Do the math for me.
And if nothing breaks all year, I just paid for nothing?
delivery.speaker: primary

resolution.concern: They believe paying for problems as they come is cheaper than paying for prevention, and they do not want a charge for something they may not use.
resolvedBy: Agreeing it is a reasonable approach for some homes
Doing the honest math, what the plan costs against what it saves for their equipment
Pointing to the specific reason in their home, such as an older water heater or high water pressure, without exaggerating
Accepting the no and leaving the details with them

evaluate.pass: The tech agrees it can be a reasonable choice, does the honest math for this home, and accepts the answer without pushing.
evaluate.fail: The tech predicts a breakdown to scare them, argues the math without real numbers, or asks again after a clear no.

coaching.why: Paying as you go is a reasonable plan for many homes, and pretending otherwise costs you credibility. The membership is worth it when this home has a specific reason, such as older equipment or hard water, and the math shows it. If the reason is not there, saying so makes them more likely to call you next time.
coaching.modelResponse: That's fair, and for some homes it's the right call. Here's the honest math for yours: what the plan costs a year, against what the flush and the repair discount would save on a water heater this age. If it doesn't come out ahead for you, skip it. I'll leave the details either way.
commonMistakes: Predicting a breakdown to create urgency
Talking about savings without real numbers
Asking again after a clear no
Treating the customer's approach as foolish

review.author: Claude
notes: Company specs supply the plan's yearly price and repair discount so the tech can do this math with real numbers.

moves.name: Can't you just repair it?
moves.summary: The tech recommends replacement and the customer asks whether it can be repaired instead.

delivery.intent: Ask whether it can just be repaired instead of replaced. Sound hopeful and a little doubtful of the recommendation. You are not hostile. You just do not want to spend more than you need to. Do not say how much you hoped to spend unless the tech asks. If the tech shows you the problem or offers a real repair, accept their answer. If they only say it cannot be fixed, ask once more.
lines: Can't you just fix it? I don't want to replace the whole thing.
Isn't there a part you can swap out instead of buying a whole new one?
It was working fine last week. Seems like it just needs a repair.
I'd rather just repair it for now, if that's possible. Is it?
followUps: Somebody fixed my last one for a couple hundred bucks.
Are you sure? Or is replacing it just easier for you?
delivery.speaker: primary

resolution.concern: They suspect replacement is the more profitable answer, not the necessary one, and they do not want to throw away something that might still work.
resolvedBy: Answering honestly whether a repair is possible here
Offering the repair as a real option when it is one, with how long it should last
Showing why when it cannot be repaired, with the part, a photo, or a reading
Comparing repairing now and replacing later in plain numbers
Letting them choose

evaluate.pass: The tech says honestly whether a repair will work here, offers it when it is real, and shows the evidence when it is not.
evaluate.fail: The tech refuses a repair that would work, invents a reason it cannot be fixed, or agrees to a repair that will not hold just to keep the customer happy.

coaching.why: This question tests whether replacement is your honest recommendation. When a repair is a real option, offering it builds more trust than any sale. When it is not, the customer needs to see why, not just hear it.
coaching.modelResponse: Fair question. If a repair will hold, that's what I'll recommend, and I'll tell you how long I'd expect it to last. If it won't, I'll show you why. Here, the leak is coming from the tank itself. Come take a look at the rust at the bottom seam. There's no part that fixes a leaking tank. Does that make sense?
commonMistakes: Pushing replacement when a repair would honestly hold
Saying it cannot be fixed without showing why
Agreeing to a patch that will not last to avoid an argument
Leaving out how long a repair is likely to last

review.author: Claude
notes: The model response uses the leaking-tank case. In wh-repair-or-replace-9yr the repair is the honest answer, and the pass and fail lines cover both cases.

moves.name: Just do the cheap fix
moves.summary: After hearing the options and prices, the customer asks for the cheapest fix and nothing more.

delivery.intent: Tell the tech you want the cheapest way to deal with it, or ask for the bare minimum that gets it working. You mean it: money matters more to you today than a longer warranty or extras. Do not explain your money situation unless the tech asks. Ask straight out whether the cheap option will actually work. If the tech answers honestly and states the trade-off once, accept that. If the tech pushes the bigger option again without a new reason, hold your position more firmly.
lines: Just do the cheapest one. I don't need anything fancy.
What's the bare minimum to get this working again?
I'll take the basic one. Whatever gets me by for now.
Can't you just do the cheap fix and call it good?
followUps: I hear you, but I still just want the cheapest one.
So is the cheap one going to work or not?
delivery.speaker: primary

resolution.concern: They need to keep this as cheap as possible and suspect the bigger options are padding. They also want to know whether the cheapest choice is actually safe or will just fail again.
resolvedBy: Saying plainly whether the cheapest option is safe and will do the job
Stating the trade-off once (lifespan, warranty, what could happen) without scare talk
Respecting the choice and offering to do the basic option well
Saying no clearly, with the reason, if the shortcut they want is unsafe or not to code

evaluate.pass: The tech says honestly whether the cheapest option is sound, states the trade-off once, and respects the choice, or explains plainly why a requested shortcut is unsafe or not to code.
evaluate.fail: The tech keeps pushing the bigger option, uses scare talk, or agrees to skip a safety or code item to hit the customer's number.

coaching.why: Choosing the cheapest option is a legitimate decision, and customers often have reasons they have not shared. Your job is to make sure the choice is safe and understood, then respect it. Pushing harder tells the customer the other options were about the sale.
coaching.modelResponse: That's a fair choice. The basic option fixes the problem and meets code, so it's safe. The trade-off is a shorter warranty, and it may not last as long. If that fits right now, I'll do it right. The only things I won't skip are the code and safety items, and I'll show you exactly which those are.
commonMistakes: Pitching the bigger option again with the same reasons
Using worst-case stories to scare them off the basic option
Agreeing to skip a code or safety item to hit their number
Treating the basic choice as a mistake they will regret

review.author: Claude
notes: Pairs with the the-cheap-fix drill. Differs from just-repair-it (scope), which is about repairing instead of replacing.
The model response assumes the basic option meets code. Scenarios where the cheapest option is not safe should say so in findings so the Coach can judge the honest answer.

moves.name: The last company ripped me off
moves.summary: Early in the visit, the customer says a previous company overcharged them or did work that did not hold up.

delivery.intent: Tell the tech, early and a little guarded, that the last company you used overcharged you or did work that did not last, so you are going to be careful this time. Keep it calm and factual, not a rant. Give one short detail only if asked, such as what they charged or what went wrong. Become friendlier only if the tech listens, does not criticize the other company, and explains in specific terms how this visit will work.
lines: Just so you know, the last company we had out here ripped us off.
I'll be honest, I don't trust plumbers much. The last guy overcharged me big time.
We paid a company a lot of money last year, and it broke again a month later.
The last outfit we called charged us a fortune and didn't fix anything.
followUps: That's what they said too, though.
So how is this going to be any different?
delivery.speaker: primary

resolution.concern: They were overcharged or let down before and expect it to happen again. They need to see, in specific terms, how this visit protects them: what they will see, approve, and get in writing.
resolvedBy: Listening to what happened and acknowledging it without judging the other company
Asking what went wrong
Explaining how this visit will work, so they see what is found, get the price before any work, and approve everything first
Following through on that during the rest of the call

evaluate.pass: The tech listens, acknowledges what happened without criticizing the other company, asks what went wrong, and explains how this visit will work so the customer sees and approves everything first.
evaluate.fail: The tech moves on without responding to it, criticizes the other company, or says "we're not like them" without saying what will be different.

coaching.why: A customer who was overcharged before is telling you what they need: proof, not promises. Agreeing that the last company was bad does not build trust, but showing them how this visit works does. What you do during the rest of the call is what answers the worry.
coaching.modelResponse: I'm sorry that happened. That's a lousy feeling. Can I ask what went wrong? (Listens.) Here's how I work. I'll show you everything I find, explain it in plain words, and you'll have the price in writing before I touch anything. If you decide not to do anything, that's okay too. Fair enough?
commonMistakes: Criticizing the other company
Saying "we're not like them" without explaining what is different
Skipping past the story to start the inspection
Getting defensive, as if the customer is accusing you

review.author: Claude
notes: This is the calm objection. The emotional version is the angry-about-last-company behavior move. Consider excluding one in scenarios that force the other.

moves.name: Let me call you back
moves.summary: When asked to decide, the customer tries to end the visit by saying they will call back later.

delivery.intent: Say you will call them back, in a way that makes clear you want the visit to wrap up. You are not ready, and you have not said why. Do not give a reason unless the tech asks a good question; if they do, give a real one (a question about the price, whether it is needed, or the company). If the tech makes the next step easy and specific, agree to it.
lines: Okay, how about I just give you a call back?
Let me get back to you on this. Do you have a card?
I'll call you guys once I figure out what I want to do.
Why don't you leave me your number, and I'll call you.
followUps: Yeah, yeah, I'll call. I've got your number.
I really do need to get going, though.
delivery.speaker: primary

resolution.concern: They are not ready, and saying they will call back avoids an awkward no. Often there is an unasked question, or they plan to shop around, and they want the visit to end without pressure.
resolvedBy: Accepting it without pressure
Asking one gentle question about what would help them decide
Leaving the options and prices in writing
Setting a specific follow-up instead of an open-ended "call us"

evaluate.pass: The tech accepts it gracefully, asks one question about what would help the customer decide, and leaves written options with a specific follow-up time.
evaluate.fail: The tech makes another pitch, sounds annoyed, or leaves with only "call us" and no written options or follow-up time.

coaching.why: Many customers who say this never call back. They are ending the visit, and pushing makes them want to end it faster. Ask one honest question, then make the next step specific so a decision actually gets made.
coaching.modelResponse: Sure, no pressure at all. Before I head out, is there anything I didn't explain well, or a question that would make this easier to decide? Here are your options in writing, with the prices. Would it be all right if I followed up Thursday afternoon? And if you decide before then, just call me.
commonMistakes: Making one more pitch on the way out
Leaving with "give us a call" and no set follow-up
Treating it as a final no and leaving without asking anything

moves.name: Memberships are a scam
moves.summary: The tech offers the maintenance membership and the customer says memberships are a scam to collect money every month.

delivery.intent: Say you think service memberships are a scam. Be blunt but not rude. You have been stuck paying for subscriptions you did not use. Do not ask about the benefits yourself. Become more open only if the tech admits some memberships are not worth it, gives real numbers for your home, and is honest about how to cancel.
lines: No offense, but those memberships are a racket. I'm not signing up.
Every company has a club now. It's just a way to get money every month.
I've been burned by these before. You sign up and you can never cancel.
Memberships are how they get you. I'll pass, thanks.
followUps: So how do I cancel, if I want out?
What would I actually save in a year? Real numbers.
delivery.speaker: primary

resolution.concern: They have paid for subscriptions they never used and expect this one to be the same: a monthly charge that is hard to cancel and pays off only for the company.
resolvedBy: Agreeing that some memberships are not worth it, without getting defensive
Explaining exactly what this one includes and what it costs for the year
Showing what it would save or prevent for their equipment, in real numbers
Explaining plainly how to cancel
Saying so if it does not make sense for them

evaluate.pass: The tech admits not every membership is worth it, explains what this one does for their home in real numbers, and says how to cancel.
evaluate.fail: The tech argues that memberships always pay off, inflates the savings, or keeps pushing after a clear no.

coaching.why: Most people have paid for a subscription they did not use, so their doubt is reasonable. A membership is worth it only if it does something specific for this home, and the customer needs to hear that in numbers. Being honest about canceling, and about when it does not pay off, makes the rest believable.
coaching.modelResponse: You're right that some aren't worth it, so let me be specific. Here's what this one covers for your house, what it costs for the year, and what it would save you. And here's exactly how you cancel. If the math doesn't work for you, skip it. I'd rather you trust me than buy it.
commonMistakes: Arguing that memberships always pay for themselves
Reading the full benefit list instead of what matters for this home
Inflating the savings or skipping how to cancel
Asking again after a clear no

review.author: Claude
notes: Company specs supply the real benefits, price, and cancellation terms the tech should cite.

moves.name: Even the monthly is too much
moves.summary: The tech offers financing, and the customer says even the monthly payment is more than they can manage.

delivery.intent: Say that even the monthly payment is more than you can manage. Sound tired and a little embarrassed, not angry. If the tech gave a specific monthly number, repeat it back. Do not share your actual budget unless the tech asks gently. If the tech offers a longer loan or more debt, say less and become more guarded. If they offer an honest cheaper way to fix it safely, you are relieved.
lines: Even by the month, that's more than I can swing right now.
I appreciate it, but another monthly payment just isn't going to work.
That would really squeeze me. I've already got a lot going out every month.
Honestly, money's tight. I can't take on another bill.
followUps: Isn't there something cheaper that would still be safe?
I don't want to sign up for something I can't keep up with.
delivery.speaker: primary

resolution.concern: Money is tight, they are embarrassed to say how tight, and they are afraid a new payment will add to bills they already struggle to pay.
resolvedBy: Acknowledging it without pity or pressure
Asking gently what amount, monthly or total, would work
Offering the least expensive option that still fixes the problem safely
Being clear about the total cost if a longer term comes up, and not pushing it
Accepting a no and making it easy to come back later

evaluate.pass: The tech acknowledges it kindly, asks what would work, and offers the least expensive safe option without pushing more debt.
evaluate.fail: The tech pushes a longer loan or a bigger payment, repeats the same offer, or makes the customer feel embarrassed.

coaching.why: When even the monthly number is too much, the customer is telling you something hard about their money. Making the loan longer to lower the payment only adds debt they cannot afford. The honest answer is the least expensive safe fix, offered without making them feel small.
coaching.modelResponse: Thank you for telling me. Let's not add a payment that makes things harder. Let me show you the least expensive way to do this safely. It may not be my first choice, but it fixes the problem. And if that's still too much right now, tell me what you can manage and I'll be straight with you about what's possible.
commonMistakes: Making the loan longer to lower the payment without explaining the total cost
Repeating the monthly number as if they did not hear it
Sounding disappointed or pitying
Treating a no as a problem to overcome instead of an answer

review.author: Claude
notes: Adds priceAboveBudget to the financing trigger so the move only fires for customers who cannot pay cash. Consider adding afterBehaviors with framed_monthly if it should fire only right after a specific monthly number.

moves.name: I need three bids
moves.summary: The customer says they always get three quotes before deciding.

delivery.intent: Say you never decide on something like this without getting at least three quotes. Be polite and matter of fact, not hostile. Do not explain the real reason unless the tech asks a good question about it.
lines: I appreciate it, but I always get three bids before I do anything like this.
This seems fine, I just want to get a couple more quotes first.
My rule is three quotes. Nothing personal.
Let me see what a couple other companies say and I'll get back to you.
followUps: I hear you, but I still want to compare.
That's what everybody says, though.
delivery.speaker: primary

resolution.concern: They want proof they are getting a fair price and fear being overcharged. More quotes are a way to feel safe, not a goal in itself.
resolvedBy: Asking what they want to learn from the other bids
Showing how the price is built and what is included
Offering a written, itemized estimate they can compare line by line
Respecting the choice and making it easy to come back

evaluate.pass: The tech respects the choice, asks what the customer wants to compare, and makes the estimate easy to compare: itemized, in writing, with what is included.
evaluate.fail: The tech drops the price to stop them shopping, pushes for a decision now, or argues that other companies are worse.

coaching.why: Three bids is almost never about three bids. It is about feeling sure the price is fair. Cutting the price confirms their fear that it was padded.
coaching.modelResponse: That makes sense, it's a real decision. Can I ask what you'll be comparing, mostly price, or what's included? Let me put everything in writing, line by line, so it's easy to hold up against the others. And if you have any questions about theirs, call me. I'll tell you straight.
commonMistakes: Dropping the price on the spot
Saying other companies cut corners
Asking for the decision again without answering the worry

review.author: Claude
notes: Gold example objection move.

moves.name: I need to think about it
moves.summary: When asked to decide, the customer says they need some time to think it over.

delivery.intent: Say you need to think it over before deciding. Be polite and vague. You have a specific worry underneath, taken from your own background (the cost, whether it all needs doing, or whether you trust the recommendation), but do not name it unless the tech asks a gentle, open question about what is on your mind. If the tech pushes for a yes, say you would rather not be rushed.
lines: Okay. I think I just need to think about it for a bit.
Let me sleep on it and I'll let you know.
This is a lot. I'd like to think it over first.
I'm not saying no. I just need a little time to think.
followUps: I just need some time, that's all.
I'd really rather not decide this second, if that's okay.
delivery.speaker: primary

resolution.concern: Something is unresolved, usually the money, whether the work is really needed, or whether they trust the recommendation. "Think about it" is a polite way to avoid naming it.
resolvedBy: Respecting the request instead of pushing
Asking gently what they want to think through, so the real question comes out
Answering that question directly
Leaving the options in writing with a specific next step if they still want time

evaluate.pass: The tech respects the request, asks gently what the customer wants to think through, answers it, and if they still want time, leaves the options in writing with a specific next step.
evaluate.fail: The tech pushes for a decision now, uses a deadline or scare talk, or repeats the pitch without finding out what is holding the customer back.

coaching.why: "I need to think about it" usually means there is a question the customer has not asked. Pushing makes a no more likely, and leaving without asking means the question never gets answered. Ask once, gently, what they want to think through, then answer that.
coaching.modelResponse: Of course. It's a real decision, and I don't want you to feel rushed. Can I ask what part you're still weighing? Is it the cost, or whether it all needs doing? If I can answer it now, great. If not, I'll leave everything in writing and give you a call tomorrow, or whenever works for you.
commonMistakes: Saying "what's there to think about?"
Creating a deadline or a today-only price to force a decision
Leaving without asking what is holding them back
Leaving with no written options and no follow-up plan

moves.name: After my next paycheck
moves.summary: When asked to decide, the customer asks to wait until their next paycheck or check arrives.

delivery.intent: Ask to wait until your next paycheck or check comes in, in a week or two, before doing the work. Use the words that fit your life: payday, your check, or your Social Security deposit. You do want the work done; the money is just not there today. Do not say how much you have now unless the tech asks with care. If the tech offers to book it for after payday, or gives a specific monthly number without pushing, consider it seriously.
lines: Can we do this after I get paid on Friday?
My check comes in on the first. Could it wait till then?
I get paid next week. Can we put it on the schedule after that?
I want to do it, I just don't have it until payday.
followUps: I'd rather wait than put it on a card.
It's only a week or so. Is that really a problem?
delivery.speaker: primary

resolution.concern: They want the work done but do not have the cash until payday, and they do not want to take on debt or be left without enough for other bills.
resolvedBy: Respecting the cash timing without pressure or judgment
Saying honestly whether waiting a week or two is safe, and what to do until then
Offering to book the work for right after payday if waiting is safe
Explaining a specific monthly option with plain terms, if it helps, without pushing it

evaluate.pass: The tech says honestly whether a short wait is safe, offers to book the work for right after payday, and mentions a specific monthly option without pushing it.
evaluate.fail: The tech invents urgency to get it done today, keeps pushing financing after the customer says they would rather wait, or makes the customer feel judged about money.

coaching.why: This customer has already said yes to the work; the only question is when. If a week or two is safe, book the date and keep the job. If it is not safe, explain why plainly and show what would make it possible now.
coaching.modelResponse: That's completely fair. Waiting a week is safe here, and I'll tell you what to watch for until then. Let's put you on the schedule for right after payday so it's set. If you'd rather not wait, I can show you the exact monthly payment instead. Either way works for me.
commonMistakes: Inventing urgency so the job happens today
Leaving without booking a date
Pushing financing after the customer said they would rather wait

review.author: Claude
notes: Persona list is limited to registry personas with a named money squeeze. Widen it if other personas get tight cash in their backgrounds.
Uses priceAboveBudget so it fires only when the price is above the persona's cash budget. The model response assumes a short wait is safe; scenarios with urgent findings change the honest answer.

moves.name: Just fix what I called about
moves.summary: The tech brings up findings beyond the reason for the call, and the customer asks them to fix only what they called about.

delivery.intent: Tell the tech you only want the problem you called about fixed. Be polite and firm. You feel a sales pitch coming. Do not ask about the other finding unless the tech explains it once in a way that sounds honest and not pushy. If the tech accepts your choice right away, relax and listen. If they bring it up again, answer in fewer words and sound irritated.
lines: I just want you to fix what I called about. That's it.
Can we just stick to what I called you out for?
Look, I appreciate it, but I only need the one thing fixed today.
Every time someone comes out, it turns into a whole list. Just the one thing, please.
followUps: Is that a real problem, or just something you noticed?
If it's been fine this long, it can wait, right?
delivery.speaker: primary

resolution.concern: They feel the visit turning into a sales pitch and are afraid of a bill that keeps growing. They want control over what gets done in their home.
resolvedBy: Agreeing right away to fix what they called about
Mentioning the other finding once, plainly, with evidence and its real urgency
Saying clearly when something is a safety issue, without exaggerating
Writing it down and leaving the decision with them

evaluate.pass: The tech agrees to fix what they called about, explains the other finding once with its real urgency, and leaves the choice with the customer.
evaluate.fail: The tech keeps pushing the extra work, makes it sound more urgent than it is, or makes the customer feel difficult for saying no.

coaching.why: The customer is protecting themselves from a visit that grows into a big bill. Agreeing first makes them willing to listen, and one clear explanation is enough. If a finding is a real safety issue, saying so plainly is your job, but repeating it until they agree is pressure.
coaching.modelResponse: Of course, that's what I'm here for, and I'll take care of it. One thing I want you to know about, and then it's your call. Your main water shutoff is stuck and won't turn. Here's a photo. It's not urgent today, but if a pipe ever breaks, you couldn't shut the water off. I'll note it on your invoice.
commonMistakes: Bringing the extra finding up again after the customer said no
Making a minor finding sound urgent
Leaving out a real safety issue to avoid the conversation
Acting annoyed that the customer said no

review.author: Claude
notes: The model response uses the stuck main shutoff from main-shutoff-seized. The pattern is the same for failing shutoff valves or a worn anode rod.

moves.name: I paid less last time
moves.summary: The customer says they paid much less the last time they had this kind of work done.

delivery.intent: Say you paid a lot less the last time you had this kind of work done, years ago or at a previous house. You remember the number roughly and you are sure it was lower. Do not bring up what was included last time. If the tech asks, admit you are not sure it had the same parts, a permit, or the same warranty.
lines: I had this same thing done a few years back and paid way less.
Last time I had one of these put in, it was like half that.
Huh. I paid nowhere near that the last time.
That's a lot more than I paid at my old house.
followUps: Prices can't have gone up that much.
It was the same job, though. Why's it so much more now?
delivery.speaker: primary

resolution.concern: The jump makes them think they are being overcharged. They are comparing to a remembered number, not to the same job, and they need a reason the difference is fair.
resolvedBy: Asking when it was done and what was included last time
Explaining honestly what has changed, such as parts costs, code requirements, and permits
Showing what this price includes that the last job may not have
Not arguing with their memory or criticizing whoever did the last job

evaluate.pass: The tech asks when the last job was done and what it included, then explains honestly what is different now and what this price covers.
evaluate.fail: The tech argues with the customer's memory, makes up reasons for the difference, or criticizes whoever did the last job.

coaching.why: Customers compare to the last number they remember, not to the same job. Often the old job was years ago, had no permit, or left out items code now requires. Ask about the last job first, then explain the difference honestly, without criticizing the last company.
coaching.modelResponse: That's a fair thing to compare. When was that, and do you remember what was included? Was there a permit? (Listens.) Okay. A few things are different now. This job needs a couple of code items that weren't required back then, and parts cost more than they did. Let me show you each piece so you can compare it with what you got.
commonMistakes: Telling the customer their memory must be wrong
Saying the last company must have skipped things, without knowing
Explaining price increases at length instead of asking about the last job

review.author: Claude
notes: The model response assumes this job includes code items newer than the customer's last job, which is true for California water heater replacements. The Coach should accept any honest, specific explanation of the difference.

moves.name: I was quoted less on the phone
moves.summary: The customer says the office gave them a lower number on the phone than the price the tech just gave.

delivery.intent: Say that when you called, whoever answered gave you a much lower number or range. You are irritated and wonder if this is a bait and switch. Stay vague about exactly what was said (a starting price, a ballpark, or just the fee to come out) unless the tech asks. Do not claim it was a written quote. Calm down if the tech takes you seriously, does not tell you that you misheard, and explains the difference plainly.
lines: Hold on. The person on the phone told me it'd be a lot less than that.
When I called, they said these usually run way under that.
That's not what your office told me. They gave me a much lower number.
Wait, I was told on the phone it'd be around half that.
followUps: So your office just gave me a number that means nothing?
Then why would they tell me that? That doesn't feel right.
delivery.speaker: primary

resolution.concern: They feel tricked: a low number got them to book the visit, and now the real price is much higher. They want to know whether they are being misled, and whether anything else will change before the job is done.
resolvedBy: Not denying or arguing with what they were told
Explaining honestly that a phone number is usually a starting range given before anyone has seen the job
Showing exactly what is different about their job and what the price includes
Offering to check what was said on the call, without blaming the office
Putting the price in writing so it does not change again

evaluate.pass: The tech takes the complaint seriously, does not deny what the customer heard, explains honestly why this job's price differs, and offers to check what was said on the call.
evaluate.fail: The tech tells the customer they misheard, makes up a story about what the office said or meant, blames the office, or argues about the number.

coaching.why: To the customer, a price well above the phone number looks like a bait and switch. You were not on that call, so you cannot say what was promised. Being honest about how phone numbers work, and showing exactly what is different about this job, is what rebuilds trust.
coaching.modelResponse: I'm glad you told me, and I can see why that's frustrating. I wasn't on that call, so I won't guess what was said, but I'll check. Usually a phone number is a starting range before anyone has seen the job. Here's what's different with yours and everything that's in this price. It's in writing, so it won't change on you.
commonMistakes: Telling the customer they must have misheard
Blaming the office with "they shouldn't have told you that"
Matching the phone number on the spot without knowing what was said
Getting defensive about the price

review.author: Claude
notes: Whether a company honors a number given on the phone is company policy. Add each company's answer to its objectionAnswers.
Check the "starting range" wording against how each company's office actually quotes on the phone.

moves.name: I'm selling soon
moves.summary: The customer plans to sell the house in about two years and does not want to put money into it.

delivery.intent: Say you are selling in about two years and do not want to put real money into the house. Be friendly but firm. You want the cheapest thing that works until you list. Do not mention that you worry about what a buyer's inspector will find. Admit it if the tech asks about the sale or your plans. If the tech keeps pushing the top option, give short answers and lose interest.
lines: I'm selling in a couple of years. I'm not putting real money into this place.
I'm out of here in about two years. What's the cheapest thing that gets me there?
Why would I spend that on a house I'm about to sell?
Honestly, the next owner can deal with it. I just need it working till I list.
followUps: The buyer's not going to care about that, are they?
Just give me the bare minimum. What's the least I can do?
delivery.speaker: primary

resolution.concern: He does not want to spend on a house he is leaving, and he suspects the tech is using the sale to sell him more. He also wants to avoid surprises that could hurt the sale.
resolvedBy: Taking the two-year plan seriously and changing the recommendation to fit it
Recommending the lowest honest option for a short stay instead of the top one
Separating what could matter at sale time, such as what a buyer's inspector may find, from what will not
Sending disclosure questions to his real estate agent instead of guessing
Not using the sale to create fear

evaluate.pass: The tech changes the recommendation to fit the two-year plan, points to the option that fits it, and explains plainly what could matter when he sells.
evaluate.fail: The tech keeps pushing the top option, uses the sale to scare him, or guesses at disclosure rules.

coaching.why: A customer who is leaving is telling you what he values: getting to the sale without surprises. Recommending less when less fits proves your other recommendations are honest. What could matter at sale time is what a buyer's inspector may find, and that is worth explaining calmly.
coaching.modelResponse: That changes what I'd recommend. For two years, you don't need the top option or the longest warranty. The basic fix does the job. The one thing I'd think about is the sale itself. A buyer's inspector may find this, so fixing it now could cost less than a credit later. Your agent can tell you which is better.
commonMistakes: Pushing the top option on someone leaving in two years
Using the sale as a scare tactic, such as saying the house will not sell
Guessing at disclosure law instead of sending them to their agent
Ignoring the plan and repeating the original recommendation

review.author: Claude
notes: Written for greg-selling. Check the two-year timeline against his persona file once it exists.

If a water heater scenario is added for greg-selling, California sellers must certify in writing that the water heater is braced or strapped (Health and Safety Code 19211). Left out of the model response so the tech does not give legal advice.

moves.name: Put it in writing
moves.summary: Before agreeing, the customer asks for the work and the price in writing.

delivery.intent: Say you will not agree to anything until you see the price and exactly what is included in writing. You have had surprise charges added before, or you just want something to hold them to. Relax when the tech agrees right away, itemizes it, and says what could change the price and that you would approve any change first. If the tech hesitates or wants to start first, get firmer.
lines: Before I agree to anything, I want all of that in writing.
Can you write that up for me? Every line, with the total.
I don't do anything on a handshake anymore. Put it on paper for me.
I'll need that in writing first, with exactly what's included.
followUps: And that's the final price? Nothing extra at the end?
What if you open it up and find something else?
delivery.speaker: primary

resolution.concern: They have had surprise charges or vague promises before. They want the scope and the price fixed so neither can grow once work starts.
resolvedBy: Agreeing right away, without hesitation
Itemizing the work, the price, and the warranty in writing
Saying plainly what could change the price and that any change needs their approval first
Giving them time to read it before signing

evaluate.pass: The tech agrees right away, writes out the work and the price line by line, and explains what could change it and that the customer approves any change first.
evaluate.fail: The tech hesitates, pushes to start before anything is written, or gives a loose number that could grow later.

coaching.why: Asking for it in writing is a reasonable request, and a careful customer will not say yes without it. Any hesitation looks like you plan to change the price later. Agree right away, then answer the question behind it: what happens if you find something else.
coaching.modelResponse: Absolutely, you should have it in writing. I'll list every part of the job, the price, and the warranty. That price is for the job as written. If I open it up and find something I couldn't see, I stop and show you, and nothing extra happens unless you approve it. Take your time reading it.
commonMistakes: Saying "we'll figure out the final number when I'm done"
Pushing to start work before the estimate is written
Leaving out what could change the price

review.author: Claude
notes: The model response assumes the company gives written, upfront prices and gets approval before any change. Confirm against each company's process.

moves.name: I need to talk to my spouse
moves.summary: When asked to decide, the customer says they need to talk it over with their spouse or partner first.

delivery.intent: Say you cannot decide this without talking to your spouse or partner first. Call them by name if your background gives one. It is true: you make big money decisions together. Do not commit to a yes on your own, even if the tech is good. If the tech offers a way to include your partner, such as a quick call, photos, or the options in writing, take it seriously.
lines: I can't make this call without talking to my other half first.
We make big decisions like this together. Let me talk it over tonight.
I'd have to run it by my partner. That's a lot of money for us.
Let me talk it over at home tonight, and we'll give you a call.
followUps: I hear you, but I'm not deciding this without them.
It's not that I don't trust you. We just do these things together.
delivery.speaker: primary

resolution.concern: They share big money decisions with their partner and will not commit without them. They may also worry about explaining it well enough at home, or being blamed if it turns out to be the wrong call.
resolvedBy: Respecting that they decide together
Offering to include the partner now with a quick call, or with photos and a short written summary
Making sure the customer can explain what was found, the options, and the prices
Setting a specific time to follow up with both of them

evaluate.pass: The tech respects the joint decision, offers a way to include the partner now or makes it easy to explain later, and sets a specific follow-up.
evaluate.fail: The tech pushes the customer to decide alone, suggests the partner does not need a say, or uses a deadline or discount to force a yes.

coaching.why: When a couple decides together, this is not a stall. It is how they make decisions, and pushing for a yes asks the customer to decide without their partner. Make it easy to bring the other person in now, or to explain it accurately later.
coaching.modelResponse: That makes sense, it's a big decision for both of you. Would it help to call them now? I can explain it to them in two minutes. If that doesn't work, I'll send you a photo of what I found and the options in writing, so you're not explaining it from memory. What time tonight is good for me to check back?
commonMistakes: Asking "can't you just decide?" or implying the partner does not need a say
Leaving with nothing the customer can show their partner
Offering a discount if they sign before their partner gets home
Not setting a time to follow up

review.author: Claude
notes: Fires only when the second person is not in the room (secondaryPresent false). Pairs with the the-spouse-stall and bring-in-the-second-decision-maker drills.
Lines avoid naming a gender so the scripted voice works for every listed persona. Confirm jen-busy-parent gets a secondary person when that persona is written.

moves.name: That's too expensive
moves.summary: The customer reacts to the price by saying it costs too much.

delivery.intent: React to the price by saying it is too much. Say it from your own situation, in your own words, not as a bargaining move. Do not ask for a discount. Do not say what you can afford, what number you had in mind, or what else is going on with money unless the tech asks a good question about it. If the tech drops the price right away, trust the rest of the estimate less.
lines: [exhales] Wow. That's a lot more than I was expecting.
That's way too much for something like this.
Hm. That's too expensive. I can't do that.
Honestly, that seems like a lot of money for what it is.
followUps: I get that, but it's still a lot of money.
Okay, but that doesn't really change the number for me.
delivery.speaker: primary

resolution.concern: The number is bigger than they planned for, and they are not sure it is worth it or that they can cover it without strain. "Too expensive" is a first reaction that usually means a budget limit or doubt about the value.
resolvedBy: Asking what feels like too much, the total itself or not being sure it is worth it
Explaining in plain words what the price covers and why
Showing an honest lower-cost option that still solves the problem
Giving a specific monthly number when the total is the barrier

evaluate.pass: The tech stays calm, asks what feels like too much, explains what the price covers, and offers an honest lower-cost option or a monthly number if the total is the problem.
evaluate.fail: The tech knocks money off on the spot, drops needed work to hit a number, pushes for a yes anyway, or argues that the price is fair.

coaching.why: "Too expensive" is usually a first reaction, not a final answer. Underneath it is a budget limit or doubt that the work is worth it, and you cannot tell which until you ask. Dropping the price confirms the number was padded, and defending it starts an argument.
coaching.modelResponse: I understand, it's a real number. Can I ask what feels like too much? Is it the total, or not being sure it's worth it? (Listens.) Okay. There's a lower option that still fixes it safely, and I'll show you exactly what you'd give up. And if spreading it out helps, I can give you an exact monthly number.
commonMistakes: Knocking money off before finding out what the concern is
Defending the price at length before asking a single question
Jumping straight to financing without asking what the worry is
Pitching the same option again with the same reasons

review.author: Claude
notes: Check that perception tags a discount offered right after this objection as discounted_unprompted, since the customer did not ask for one.

moves.name: What am I paying for?
moves.summary: The customer asks what is actually included in the price.

delivery.intent: Ask what exactly is in that price. You are not refusing; you want to know where the money goes before you agree. If the tech gives a vague answer like "parts and labor," ask for more detail. If the tech uses trade words, ask what they mean. Do not mention other quotes or what you think it should cost.
lines: Okay, but what am I actually paying for there?
Can you break that down for me? What's in that number?
That's a lot. Where does all that money go?
So what does that include? Is that everything?
followUps: Okay, but parts and labor doesn't really tell me anything.
So if I add it all up, where's the rest of it going?
delivery.speaker: primary

resolution.concern: They cannot see where the money goes, so the price feels made up. They want to know what they are getting, and that nothing is hidden or padded.
resolvedBy: Walking through what the price covers in plain words, such as the parts, labor, code items, permit, haul-away, and warranty
Saying what is not included and what could change the price
Offering to put it in writing, itemized
Checking whether the breakdown answered the question

evaluate.pass: The tech breaks the price into plain parts (parts, labor, code items, permit, haul-away, warranty), says what is not included, and offers it in writing.
evaluate.fail: The tech answers with "parts and labor," lists trade terms without explaining them, makes up a cost breakdown, or gets short with the customer for asking.

coaching.why: A price with no breakdown feels made up, even when it is fair. A customer who asks this is often close to yes and wants to see where the money goes. A clear, itemized answer gives them something they can check.
coaching.modelResponse: Good question. It breaks down into the parts, the labor to do it, anything code requires, the permit if there is one, haul-away, and the warranty on parts and labor. I'll write it out line by line so you can see every piece, and what isn't included. Does that answer it, or is there a piece you want me to go into?
commonMistakes: Saying "parts and labor" and stopping there
Listing trade terms the customer does not know
Taking the question as an attack on the price
Guessing at a dollar split they cannot back up

review.author: Claude
notes: Flat-rate techs often do not know the dollar split per line item. The model response lists what is included without inventing per-line costs; company price books may allow more detail.
passIf requires justified_value plus one of the plain-language behaviors. Confirm the engine reads allBehaviors and anyBehaviors together that way.

moves.name: What do I actually get?
moves.summary: The tech offers the membership and the customer asks what they would actually get for the money.

delivery.intent: Ask what you would actually get from the membership. Sound interested but unconvinced, like someone who has heard a vague pitch before. Do not accept a list of perks. Become more interested only if the tech names what it does for your equipment and what it would have saved you today. If the tech reads a long list, lose interest.
lines: Okay, but what do I actually get for that?
Sounds nice, but what does it actually do for me?
So what's in it, really? Like, specifically for my house.
Break it down for me. What exactly am I paying for?
followUps: And what's not included? There's always something.
Would I have saved anything today if I'd had it?
delivery.speaker: primary

resolution.concern: They cannot tell what they would be paying for. They want specifics that apply to their home and an honest sense of whether it pays off.
resolvedBy: Naming the two or three benefits that matter for their home, not the full list
Putting it in numbers, what it costs a year and what it would save
Connecting it to what was found today
Saying plainly what it does not cover

evaluate.pass: The tech names the benefits that matter for this home, puts them in numbers, and says plainly what the plan does not cover.
evaluate.fail: The tech reads the whole benefit list, inflates the savings, or cannot say what is not included.

coaching.why: This is a buying question, and most techs answer it by reading the benefit list. The customer wants to know what changes for their house and whether the math works. Two or three specific benefits tied to today's visit do more than the full list.
coaching.modelResponse: For your house, it comes down to three things. A yearly check on the water heater, which matters because yours is getting older. Priority when something breaks, so you're not waiting days. And the member discount, which would have taken a real amount off today's bill. I'll show you the number. And here's what it doesn't cover, so there are no surprises.
commonMistakes: Reading the full benefit list
Giving no numbers for cost or savings
Skipping what the plan does not cover
Promising savings the customer will not see

review.author: Claude
notes: The model response assumes a yearly water heater check, priority service, and a repair discount. Company specs supply the actual benefits and numbers.

moves.name: What's the catch?
moves.summary: The tech offers financing and the customer asks what the catch is: the credit check, the interest, and what happens if they fall behind.

delivery.intent: Ask what the catch is with the financing. Be skeptical but fair. You have heard stories about interest that shows up later and surprise fees. Ask about the credit check, the interest rate, and what happens if the balance is not paid off in time. Accept clear, honest answers. Get more suspicious if the tech says there is no catch at all or cannot answer.
lines: Okay, that sounds easy. So what's the catch?
There's always a catch with these payment plans. What is it?
What happens if I miss a payment or can't pay it off in time?
Does this run my credit? And what's the interest, really?
followUps: So if I'm a month late paying it off, what happens?
Is all of that in writing somewhere I can read?
delivery.speaker: primary

resolution.concern: They suspect the easy monthly number hides interest, fees, or a hit to their credit, and they do not want to be trapped in a loan they did not understand.
resolvedBy: Explaining the real terms in plain words, including the credit check, the rate, the term, and the total cost
Saying exactly what happens if a promotional balance is not paid off in time
Showing the lender's written terms instead of summarizing from memory
Saying "I'll find out" when unsure instead of guessing

evaluate.pass: The tech explains the credit check, the rate, the term, and what happens if a promotional balance is not paid off, and shows the written terms.
evaluate.fail: The tech says there is no catch, guesses at the terms, or skips the credit check and interest to keep the sale moving.

coaching.why: Most people have heard about interest that shows up later and surprise fees, so honest terms are what they want. Saying there is no catch loses them, because there is almost always a credit check and usually interest somewhere. Plain terms, in writing, make the monthly number believable.
coaching.modelResponse: Fair question, and you should ask it. You'd apply with the lender, so there's a credit check. If you're approved, the payment is the monthly number I gave you, and here are the rate and the term in writing. On a promo plan, the big one is what happens if it's not paid off in time, so let's read that line together.
commonMistakes: Saying there's no catch
Guessing at the rate or promo terms from memory
Skipping the credit check because it might scare them off
Using terms like APR or deferred interest without explaining them

review.author: Claude
notes: Real lender terms belong in each company's spec. The model response assumes a lender application with a credit check. Confirm against each company's financing partner.

moves.name: You guys always upsell
moves.summary: The customer says plumbing companies always try to sell more than the job needs.

delivery.intent: Say, a little sharply, that companies like this always try to sell you more than you need. Say it when the tech mentions anything beyond the problem you called about or lays out bigger options; if they have not yet, say it as a warning. You cannot tell which recommendations are real. Relax only if the tech clearly separates what is required from what is optional and offers the smallest honest fix. If the tech recommends something the findings do not support, say so directly.
lines: Here we go. You guys always find something else to sell me.
I called about one thing, and now it's three things?
Every time somebody comes out here, it turns into a bigger job.
Is all of that really needed, or is this the upsell part?
followUps: So which of those do I actually need? Just tell me straight.
That still sounds like a sales pitch to me.
delivery.speaker: primary

resolution.concern: They have been sold extras before and cannot tell which recommendations are real. They want to know what is truly required, and to feel free to say no to the rest.
resolvedBy: Separating what is required (failing, unsafe, or required by code) from what is optional, in plain words
Showing the evidence for anything called required
Offering the smallest honest fix as a real option
Saying out loud that the optional items are the customer's call, and meaning it

evaluate.pass: The tech separates what is required from what is optional, shows the evidence for the required items, offers the smallest honest fix, and makes clear the extras are the customer's choice.
evaluate.fail: The tech gets defensive, calls everything necessary without showing why, keeps pushing work the findings do not support, or drops a real code or safety item to look less pushy.

coaching.why: This customer has been sold things they did not need, and saying you are different will not change their mind. Seeing you separate required work from optional work will. Show the evidence, offer the smallest honest fix, and let them choose.
coaching.modelResponse: That's fair, and I'd rather you ask. Here's the straight version. This part is required because it's failing, and I'll show you. This one is required by code, so I can't leave it out. Everything else is optional, and it's completely your call. If you only want the required part, that's a complete fix, and I'll do it right.
commonMistakes: Saying "we're not like other companies" instead of showing it
Calling optional items "needed" to keep them in the quote
Getting defensive about the question
Dropping a real code or safety item to look less pushy

review.author: Claude
notes: Differs from only-fix-what-i-called-for (scope), which limits the work. This one questions the tech's motive.

moves.name: Angry about the last company
moves.summary: The customer gets heated about what the last company did to them, and some of that anger lands on this tech.

delivery.intent: Unload about the last company that worked on your house. You are angry at them, not at this tech, but some of it spills over. Say what happened in two or three sentences, with real feeling, and do not hold back. You are watching how this tech reacts. Calm down a little if they let you finish, ask what happened, and acknowledge it without bashing the other company or making big promises. Get more guarded if they cut you off, defend the industry, or promise it will never happen with them.
lines: The last company charged me nine hundred dollars, and it broke again two weeks later.
The last guy told me I needed a whole new system. I didn't. I found out later.
[frustrated] I've been burned, okay? The last plumber left a mess and never called back.
They charged me for three hours and he was here forty minutes. So yeah, I'm a little touchy.
followUps: So how do I know you're not going to do the same thing?
Everybody says that. They all say that.
delivery.speaker: primary

evaluate.pass: The tech lets the customer finish, acknowledges the frustration in plain words, asks what happened, and says specifically how this visit will work, without promises they cannot back up.
evaluate.fail: The tech cuts the customer off, rushes past it, defends the other company or the industry, or piles on about the other company.

coaching.why: An angry customer is telling you exactly what they are afraid will happen again. If you rush past it, defend the industry, or pile on the other company, you sound like the last person who came out. If you let them finish and ask what happened, you learn what this visit has to do differently, and they start to calm down.
coaching.modelResponse: That sounds really frustrating. I'm sorry that happened. Can I ask what they said was wrong? (Listens.) Here's how I work. I'll show you everything I find, and you'll get your options and prices in writing before I touch anything. If the cheaper fix is the right one, I'll tell you that.
commonMistakes: Cutting in to say "We're not like that"
Piling on about the other company
Defending the other company or the industry
Promising "That will never happen with us"

review.author: Claude
notes: Different from the trust objection last-company-ripped-me-off. This move is the emotional moment and tests listening under pressure; the objection is the calm, stated doubt that can follow.
Gated on trustBelow 50 so it fits burned customers. tasha-burned should weight it high; margaret-retiree already sets it to 0.

moves.name: Dog barking in the background
moves.summary: A dog starts barking and the customer is pulled away for a moment, missing what the tech just said.

delivery.intent: A dog starts barking nearby and takes your attention away. Deal with it in one short, distracted line, then turn back to the tech. You missed the last thing they said, and you are a little embarrassed about the noise. Pay full attention again if the tech pauses, stays relaxed, and repeats the key point briefly.
lines: Sorry, hang on. I can't hear you over that dog. Okay, go ahead.
Oh my gosh, that dog. Sorry, what were you saying?
Sorry, sorry. Give me one second. Okay, where were you?
[chuckles] Sorry. That dog never stops. Okay, go ahead.
followUps: Sorry, I missed that last part. Can you say it again?
delivery.speaker: primary

evaluate.pass: The tech stops talking for the noise, stays relaxed, and briefly repeats the last key point once the customer is back.
evaluate.fail: The tech talks over the noise as if nothing happened, or shows irritation at the interruption.

coaching.why: Noise is normal in a home, and customers are often embarrassed by it. How you handle it shows whether you are patient with their house and their life. Anything you said during the noise was not heard, so say it again briefly.
coaching.modelResponse: (Stops talking while the dog barks and waits for the customer to turn back.) "No problem at all, take your time. So, the short version of what I was saying: (the key point in one sentence). Does that make sense so far?"
commonMistakes: Raising your voice to talk over the noise
Going on with the explanation while the customer deals with the dog
Sighing or making a comment about the dog
Assuming the customer heard what you said during the barking

review.author: Claude
notes: Uses dog-bark. The lines say "that dog" so they fit the customer's own dog or a neighbor's (Margaret has a cat, not a dog).
A kids-background version would need its own move id. jen-busy-parent is the obvious fit if one is added later.

moves.name: Catches a false claim
moves.summary: Right after the tech states something false, the customer questions it directly.

delivery.intent: The tech just said something that is not true. You know enough to doubt it, because you read about it or someone told you otherwise. Question it directly but calmly. Do not explain the correct answer yet. If the tech admits they are not sure, corrects themselves, or offers to check, trust them more than before. If they double down or add more made-up detail, trust them much less.
lines: Hold on. That's not what I read. Are you sure about that?
Wait, that doesn't sound right. Where'd you get that?
Hm. My last plumber told me the opposite. Which is it?
[skeptical] Are you sure? Because I looked that up before you came.
followUps: I'm pretty sure that's not right.
So which is it? Now I'm not sure what to believe.
delivery.speaker: primary

evaluate.pass: The tech owns the mistake or the uncertainty right away, gives the correct information or offers to look it up, and does not defend the false claim.
evaluate.fail: The tech repeats the claim, adds more made-up detail to back it up, or argues with the customer to save face.

coaching.why: Getting caught in a wrong claim is recoverable. Defending it is not. A customer who catches one false statement will question every number you give after it, unless you own it right away. Saying "you're right, I misspoke" often earns back more trust than you lost.
coaching.modelResponse: You're right to question that. I said it with more confidence than I should have. I'm not certain of the exact number, and I don't want to guess on something you're paying for. Let me look it up right now, and I'll show you where it comes from.
commonMistakes: Repeating the claim more firmly
Adding made-up details to back it up
Saying "Trust me, I do this every day"
Getting defensive about the customer's research

review.author: Claude
notes: Reactive to bluffed. maxUses is 2 so a second bluff in the same call can also be caught.
paul-engineer and devin-researcher should weight this move high.

moves.name: Goes cold
moves.summary: After the tech pushes, talks down, or sounds impatient, the customer goes short and cool and starts closing the conversation.

delivery.intent: The tech just pushed you, talked down to you, or sounded impatient with you. Do not argue. Go short and cool. Answer in a few words, stop volunteering anything, and make it clear you are close to ending the visit. Warm back up slowly, and only if the tech notices, owns it plainly without excuses, and slows down. If they keep going the same way, ask them to write it up and leave.
lines: Okay. I'm not going to be rushed into this.
I was just asking a question. Okay. Go ahead.
Mm-hm. Just write it up and leave it with me.
You know, I think I'll get a couple other quotes.
followUps: I'd really just like it in writing. I'll call you.
Okay. Anything else?
delivery.speaker: primary

evaluate.pass: The tech notices the change, owns what they did in plain words, slows down, and asks what the customer needs, or leaves well if the customer wants to end the visit.
evaluate.fail: The tech keeps pushing, gets defensive, or carries on as if nothing changed.

coaching.why: When a customer goes cold, something you just did landed badly, and they decided not to argue about it. Most will not tell you. They will just say no at the end. Naming it and slowing down is the only way to get the conversation back.
coaching.modelResponse: I'm sorry, I think I came across as pushy just now, and that's not how I want this to go. There's no pressure to decide today. What questions do you still have? I'd rather you feel good about whatever you choose, even if that means getting another quote.
commonMistakes: Not noticing the shorter answers and pushing on
Explaining why you were right instead of owning it
Asking for the decision again to save the sale
Going quiet and short in return

review.author: Claude
notes: Reactive to pressured, condescended, or showed_impatience. Lines 1 and 2 fit pressure and condescension; lines 3 and 4 fit any of the three.
left_well passes because a graceful exit with a clear next step is a good outcome once the customer has gone cold.

moves.name: Half listening
moves.summary: The customer keeps checking their phone while the tech explains and misses what was just said.

delivery.intent: You are only half listening. You keep looking at your phone. Answer vaguely, or admit you missed what the tech just said. You are not rude, just busy. Give full attention again only if the tech pauses, gets your attention, and gives you the short version. If they keep explaining at full length, stay distracted.
lines: Sorry, I was reading a text. What did you say?
Mm-hm. Wait, sorry, say that last part again?
Yeah, sorry, I'm listening. Go ahead.
Huh? Sorry, I missed that. My phone keeps going off.
followUps: Sorry. What's the short version?
Okay, so what do I actually need to do?
delivery.speaker: primary

evaluate.pass: The tech notices the customer is distracted, pauses, gives the main point in one or two sentences, and checks that the customer is following.
evaluate.fail: The tech keeps explaining at full length to someone who is not listening, or makes a pointed comment about the customer's phone.

coaching.why: If the customer is not listening, nothing you explain will be remembered when it is time to decide. Talking longer does not fix it. A pause and a short version get their attention back without making them feel scolded.
coaching.modelResponse: No worries, I know you've got a lot going on. Here's the short version: (the main point in one sentence). That's the main thing you need to know. Do you want me to keep going now, or should I give you a minute to finish that first?
commonMistakes: Explaining at full length as if they heard everything
Waiting in an obvious way until they put the phone down
Saying "Am I boring you?" or another sarcastic comment
Moving on to the price while they are still distracted

review.author: Claude
notes: No sound cue. The distraction is the customer's phone screen, not a sound.

moves.name: I know what it is
moves.summary: The customer names the problem and the fix before the tech has finished looking, and expects the tech to just do it.

delivery.intent: Tell the tech what is wrong before they have finished looking, and tell them what to do about it. You are confident because you have seen this before or read about it, and you might be partly right. If the tech asks what you noticed, checks before agreeing, and shows you what they find, accept it. If they just do what you said without checking, go along with it. If they brush you off or talk down to you, dig in.
lines: I already know what it is. It's the thermostat. Just swap that out.
It's the pilot. It does this every winter. Just relight it and we're good.
It's only a clog. Run your snake down there, that's all it needs.
Honestly, it's the hard water. Everything in this house gets crusted up.
followUps: I'm telling you, that's what it is. Can't you just do that?
Okay, but how do you know it's not that?
delivery.speaker: primary

evaluate.pass: The tech takes the guess seriously, asks what the customer noticed, checks before agreeing, and if the guess is wrong, explains plainly what they actually found.
evaluate.fail: The tech does the customer's fix without checking, brushes the guess off, or argues to prove the customer wrong.

coaching.why: Customers who name the problem are often partly right, and they want credit for it. If you just do what they say, you may fix the wrong thing and they pay twice. If you brush it off, they stop trusting your diagnosis. Thank them for the clue, check it, and show them what you find.
coaching.modelResponse: That's helpful, and you might be right. What did you notice? (Listens, then checks.) The thermostat's actually working fine. The burner won't stay lit because the safety sensor next to the pilot has worn out. Here, I'll show you. Good news, that's a smaller repair than a new thermostat.
commonMistakes: Doing the fix they asked for without checking
Saying "Let me be the judge of that"
Explaining what you know instead of showing what you found
Agreeing out loud, then quietly recommending something else

review.author: Claude
notes: asked_follow_up is a pass path because in the door and discovery phases the tech has not diagnosed yet. Asking what they noticed and checking first is the right move there.
The model response calls the thermocouple "the safety sensor next to the pilot" to keep it plain.

moves.name: Cuts in to ask how much
moves.summary: While the tech is still explaining, the customer cuts in and asks how much it is.

delivery.intent: Cut in while the tech is still explaining. You are not angry. You just want to know the cost before you hear the details. Ask how much it is. If they give a number or a clear range, say okay and let them go on. If they dodge, say "it depends" with no number, or keep explaining, ask again a little more firmly.
lines: Sorry to cut you off. So how much is it?
Okay, okay. So how much is it?
So how much is it? Just ballpark.
Sorry, before you get into all that. So how much is it?
followUps: Just a ballpark. I won't hold you to it.
Okay, but what's the number?
delivery.speaker: primary

evaluate.pass: The tech calmly answers right away with a number or a clear range in plain words, then says briefly what decides the final price.
evaluate.fail: The tech sounds annoyed at being cut off, says "I'm getting to that," or keeps explaining without giving any number.

coaching.why: A customer who cuts in for the price is telling you what they need first. Making them wait sounds like you are hiding the number, and they stop listening until they hear it. A clear range answers the question, and then they are ready to hear the explanation.
coaching.modelResponse: Fair question. Depending on which way you go, it's between about (lowest option price) and (highest option price), all in. The difference is what each option includes. Give me one minute and I'll show you which one fits what you told me.
