commonMistakes: Saying "I'm getting to that" and continuing the explanation
Answering "it depends" with no number at all
Getting flustered and offering a discount before they even react
Saying the number quickly at the end of a long sentence

review.author: Claude
notes: Fires only before a price has been stated. The runtime cuts in once the tech has talked for 9 seconds.
passIf uses anyBehaviors so a plainly stated range passes even if perception does not tag it stated_price. A plain explanation with no number could also pass; check this in testing.

moves.name: One-word answers
moves.summary: The customer goes flat and answers in one or two words for a few turns, without saying why.

delivery.intent: For your next few replies, answer in one to four words and volunteer nothing. You are not angry. You are either not following, not convinced, or thinking about something else, and you do not say which. Open up again only if the tech stops explaining and asks an open question about what you think, or checks whether it makes sense. If they keep talking, stay flat.
lines: Mm-hm.
Yeah. Okay.
Sure, I guess.
Okay. Got it.
followUps: Yeah, I heard you. Anything else?
Okay. So what's next?
delivery.speaker: primary

evaluate.pass: The tech notices the short answers, stops explaining, and asks an open question or checks what the customer is thinking.
evaluate.fail: The tech keeps talking through the one-word answers, or takes "okay" as agreement and moves on to the price.

coaching.why: One-word answers mean the customer has stopped engaging, even when they are polite about it. "Okay" often means "I'm not following" or "I'm not sure," not "yes." If you keep talking, they stop listening, and you never learn what is stopping them.
coaching.modelResponse: Let me stop there, I've been doing most of the talking. What are you thinking so far? If something I said didn't make sense, or you're not sure about it, that's exactly what I want to hear. I'd rather slow down than have you feel rushed.
commonMistakes: Taking "okay" as agreement and moving on to the price
Explaining the same thing again in more detail
Asking more yes-or-no questions that get more one-word answers
Talking faster to get through it

review.author: Claude
notes: Lines are shorter than the usual 5-word minimum on purpose. One-word answers are the move.
The intent covers several replies. Check that the runtime keeps the flat style for the whole evaluation window.

moves.name: Mishears the price
moves.summary: The customer mishears the price, repeats it back wrong, or is not sure what it covers.

delivery.intent: Get the price wrong in your head. Either repeat it back wrong (for example, hearing eighteen ninety as eight ninety, or taking the total for a monthly payment), or ask whether it covers everything. Sound unsure, not suspicious. If the tech repeats the full number slowly and says what it covers, you understand. If you heard a lower number and the tech lets it stand, you believe the lower number.
lines: Sorry, did you say hundred or thousand?
Wait, is that per month, or for the whole thing?
Hold on. Say that number again? I don't think I heard it right.
Okay, so that's with everything? Or is that just the part?
followUps: Sorry, so what's the actual total? With everything?
Okay. Can you write that down for me?
delivery.speaker: primary

evaluate.pass: The tech calmly repeats the exact total and what it covers, and corrects any wrong number the customer repeated back, even a lower one.
evaluate.fail: The tech lets a wrong number stand, repeats the price with irritation or an apology, or makes the customer feel foolish for mishearing.

coaching.why: A misheard price turns into an angry customer at the end of the job, when the invoice does not match what they thought they agreed to. Repeating the full number calmly, with what it covers, protects both of you. If they heard a lower number, correcting it right away is the honest thing to do, even though it is uncomfortable.
coaching.modelResponse: Good question, let me say it again so we're on the same page. It's (the full number, said slowly), and that covers everything: parts, labor, the permit, and cleanup. That's the total, not a monthly payment. I'll write it down for you too. What questions do you have about it?
commonMistakes: Letting a lower misheard number stand to keep the mood good
Repeating the number faster, louder, or with a sigh
Saying "No, I said..." in a correcting tone
Rounding the number down while restating it

review.author: Claude
notes: Lines avoid specific numbers so the scripted voice works at any price. With Claude voicing, the intent asks for an actual misheard number.
Priority 82 sits below silence-after-price (85), which also fires after stated_price, so the silence usually wins when both are eligible.

moves.name: Mixes up the parts
moves.summary: The customer mixes up two parts or terms the tech used and builds the wrong picture of the problem.

delivery.intent: Mix up two parts or terms the tech has used, or confuse one with something you have heard of, and say it back as if you have it right. Be sincere, not joking. If the tech sorts it out in plain words without making you feel silly, you get it and feel more confident. If they use more trade terms, you stay confused. If they just agree, you keep the wrong idea.
lines: So the expansion tank, that's the same as a water softener, right?
Wait, so the anode rod is the part that heats the water?
Okay, the pressure regulator. That's the main shutoff, right?
So the sewer line, that's the pipe under the kitchen sink?
followUps: Sorry, I'm still mixing them up. Which one is the one that's broken?
Okay, so which one do I actually need?
delivery.speaker: primary

evaluate.pass: The tech kindly sorts out the two terms in plain words, says which one is the actual problem, and checks that it makes sense.
evaluate.fail: The tech lets the mix-up stand, answers with more trade terms, or makes the customer feel silly for asking.

coaching.why: A customer who mixes up two parts will decide based on the wrong picture and may feel tricked later. Getting the words straight now is part of explaining the finding. How you correct them decides whether they keep asking questions or go quiet.
coaching.modelResponse: Good question, they do sound alike. They're two different things. The expansion tank is a small tank that gives the water room to expand when it heats up, so the pressure doesn't strain your pipes. A softener takes minerals out of the water. Code requires the expansion tank. You don't need a softener for this. Want me to show you where it goes?
commonMistakes: Saying "No, that's totally different" and moving on
Correcting with more trade terms
Nodding along so the conversation keeps moving
Laughing at the mix-up before explaining

review.author: Claude
notes: Lines cover water heater, pressure, and drain jobs. With Claude voicing, the intent asks for terms the tech actually used in this call.
The model response assumes a closed system where code requires an expansion tank. Check against the company's install standard.

moves.name: My neighbor said
moves.summary: The customer repeats something a neighbor told them, with confidence, and it is wrong for this home.

delivery.intent: Repeat something your neighbor told you, with confidence, as if it settles the question. It is partly or fully wrong for your home. You like your neighbor and believe them. If the tech takes it seriously and explains plainly what is true or what is different about your home, accept it, maybe a little sheepishly. If they just agree, you believe the wrong thing. If they make you feel foolish or knock your neighbor, get defensive.
lines: My neighbor said tankless pays for itself in like two years.
My neighbor had the same thing. Their guy just relit the pilot and it was fine.
My neighbor says those expansion tanks are just an upsell.
My neighbor told me to pour that drain stuff down there once a month and you're good.
followUps: Well, it worked for them.
So you're saying my neighbor's wrong?
delivery.speaker: primary

evaluate.pass: The tech takes the neighbor's experience seriously, explains plainly what is true or what is different about this home, and keeps a correct recommendation.
evaluate.fail: The tech goes along with the wrong claim, makes fun of the neighbor's advice, or argues to win the point.

coaching.why: Advice from a neighbor comes with trust you have not earned yet. If you dismiss it, you are asking the customer to choose you over someone they know. If you go along with something wrong, it costs you later when it turns out to be wrong. Respect where it came from, then explain what is different here.
coaching.modelResponse: Tankless does save on gas, so your neighbor's right about that part. But for most homes, the savings are small next to the price difference, so it takes a lot longer than two years to make it back. I can show you the math. The real reasons people go tankless are endless hot water and space. Does either of those matter to you?
commonMistakes: Saying "Your neighbor doesn't know what they're talking about"
Agreeing to keep things friendly, then recommending the opposite
Giving a long technical lecture to prove the point
Ignoring the comment and moving on

review.author: Claude
notes: Claims cover tankless payback, pilot relights, expansion tanks, and chemical drain cleaners. All are common in Southern California homes.
The model response avoids a specific savings figure on purpose. Add one only once it is verified against current utility rates.

moves.name: Takes a phone call
moves.summary: The customer's phone rings, they say "hold on," step away for about 12 seconds, and come back having lost track of the conversation.

delivery.intent: Your phone rings. Say "hold on," say you need to take it, and step away. You are gone for the whole hold. When you come back, apologize and ask where you were. You have lost track of what the tech was saying. Pay full attention again only if the tech gives you a short recap and checks in. If they pick up in the middle of a sentence, ask them to back up.
lines: Oh, sorry, hold on. I need to take this.
Hold on one second. I've been waiting on this call.
Sorry, hold on. Let me just see who this is.
Hold on, I gotta grab this real quick. Sorry.
followUps: Sorry about that. Where were we?
Wait, sorry, back up a little. I lost track there.
delivery.speaker: primary

evaluate.pass: When the customer comes back, the tech welcomes them back, recaps the main point in a sentence or two, and checks in before going on.
evaluate.fail: The tech sounds annoyed by the wait, picks up mid-sentence as if nothing happened, or starts over from the beginning at full length.

coaching.why: After a phone call, the customer has forgotten most of what you said and is still thinking about the call. If you continue where you stopped, they nod along without following. A short recap gets their attention back on the job and shows you respect their time.
coaching.modelResponse: (Stays quiet while they are on the phone.) When they come back: "No problem at all. Real quick, here's where we were: (one sentence on the last main point, for example what you found). Does that still make sense? Any questions before I keep going?"
commonMistakes: Picking up mid-sentence as if they never left
Saying "As I was saying" in a tired voice
Continuing to explain while the customer is on the phone
Re-explaining everything from the start at full length

review.author: Claude
notes: The customer is away for holdSilenceMs. The runtime speaks followUps[0] when the hold ends, so keep it first.
Pass is judged on the tech's turns after the customer returns. A short "take your time" during the hold is fine.

moves.name: Quiet money worry
moves.summary: After the price, the customer quietly admits it is more than they can manage right now, and is embarrassed to say so.

delivery.intent: Quietly admit the price is more than you can manage right now. You are embarrassed, not angry, and you say less than you mean. Do not ask for a discount or for financing yourself. Say more about your money situation only if the tech is kind about it and does not make you feel judged. If they offer a monthly number that fits, or an honest cheaper option that still fixes the problem, you are relieved. If they push or make you feel small, shut down and say you will think about it.
lines: [hesitates] That's... um. That's more than I have right now.
I'm sorry. It's just been a tight couple of months.
Okay. I just... I don't really have that sitting around.
That's a lot for us right now. I'm kind of embarrassed to say that.
followUps: I don't want to put it on a card and be paying it off forever.
Is there anything that just gets it working for now?
delivery.speaker: primary

evaluate.pass: The tech acknowledges the worry kindly, then offers a real path: financing as a specific monthly number, or an honest lower-cost option that still solves the problem.
evaluate.fail: The tech pushes the original option anyway, makes the customer feel judged about money, or hurries past what they said.

coaching.why: Most people will not say "I can't afford it" out loud. When they hint at it, the moment is about dignity before it is about price. If you acknowledge it kindly and show a real way forward, they stay in the conversation. If they feel judged or pushed, they say they will think about it and you do not hear from them again.
coaching.modelResponse: Thank you for telling me. That's more common than you'd think, and there's nothing to be embarrassed about. Let's find what works. With financing, the option I recommended comes to about (monthly amount) a month. If you'd rather not finance, I'll walk you through the lowest-cost way to fix it safely. Which would help more?
commonMistakes: Moving past the comment and going on with the presentation
Saying "It's really not that much when you think about it"
Offering a discount instead of a real plan
Pushing financing hard before acknowledging the worry

review.author: Claude
notes: Fires after the price when the stated price is above the persona's budgetCeiling. Priority 70 puts it ahead of the price objections (about 60).
Pass needs acknowledged_feeling plus one way forward. A lower-cost option counts only when it is honest for the scenario.

moves.name: Brings back an answered objection
moves.summary: The customer brings back an objection the tech already answered, as if the answer never fully landed.

delivery.intent: The runtime picks the objection the tech answered most recently. Raise that same concern again, in new words, as if the answer did not fully settle it. You are not trying to be difficult. Either the answer did not stick, or the worry underneath is still there. Do not say the tech was wrong and do not add a new objection. If the tech answers calmly from a different angle, or asks what is still bothering you, the worry eases. If they repeat the same answer or sound impatient, it gets stronger.
lines: Sorry, I know you answered this already. I'm still stuck on it, though.
Okay, but going back to what I said before. I'm still not sure about that.
I hear you. I just keep coming back to the same thing.
Can we go back to that? It's still bugging me a little.
followUps: Yeah, that's what you said before. I'm still not sure.
I get it. It's just still on my mind.
delivery.speaker: primary

evaluate.pass: The tech stays calm and answers from a different angle (the evidence, the numbers in writing, something the customer said earlier) or asks what is still bothering them.
evaluate.fail: The tech repeats the first answer, only longer or louder, or says "like I said" or anything else that shows impatience.

coaching.why: Customers bring an objection back because the first answer did not settle the worry, not because they did not hear it. Repeating yourself, or saying "like I said," tells them you are not listening. A calm answer from a new angle, or a question about what is still bothering them, moves it forward.
coaching.modelResponse: That's fair. It's a real decision, so it makes sense it's still on your mind. Can I ask what part is still bothering you? (Listens.) Okay, let me come at it a different way. (Answers with something new: the evidence, the numbers in writing, or a detail they mentioned earlier.)
commonMistakes: Saying "like I said" or "as I mentioned"
Repeating the first answer, only longer and louder
Treating the repeat as a no and dropping the price
Answering again without asking what is still unclear

review.author: Claude
notes: trigger.when.objectionAnswered is left unset on purpose. The runtime picks the most recently answered objection, so the lines stay generic.
asked_about_concern is a second pass path alongside new_angle, since asking what is still unclear is a valid different angle.

moves.name: Goes quiet after the price
moves.summary: The customer says nothing for about six seconds after hearing the price.

delivery.intent: Say nothing. You are taking in the number. When the silence ends, react honestly to the price from your own situation, in one short sentence.
lines: Hm. Okay.
That's... a lot.
Okay. Let me think about that for a second.
[exhales] Wow.
followUps: So that's the total? Everything?
delivery.speaker: primary

evaluate.pass: The tech waits at least four seconds without restating, justifying, or lowering the price.
evaluate.fail: The tech speaks within four seconds, especially to justify, apologize for, or discount the price.

coaching.why: The silence belongs to the customer. They are doing math, not rejecting you. Filling it tells them the price is soft, and a discount offered into silence costs you money and trust at the same time.
coaching.modelResponse: (Says the price, then waits. Counts to five. Lets the customer speak first.) When they do: "Take your time. What questions do you have?"
commonMistakes: Justifying the price before they react
Saying "but we can do financing" in the first two seconds
Offering a discount into the silence

review.author: Claude
notes: Gold example behavior move. Pass and fail are measured from timing, not by a model.

moves.name: Spouse walks in
moves.summary: The other decision-maker walks in partway through, has missed everything, and asks whether it is bad.

delivery.intent: You are the other decision-maker in the house, and you just walked in partway through. You missed everything so far. Ask what is going on and whether it is bad. You will not agree to anything you do not understand. Become friendlier if the tech recaps for you in plain words and asks what you think. Get guarded if they keep talking only to your partner, re-explain everything at length, or push for a decision.
lines: Hey, sorry, I just got home. What's going on? Is it bad?
What's the plumber saying? Is it bad?
Okay, I'm here. Can somebody catch me up? How bad is it?
Wait, what did I miss? Are we talking a lot of money?
followUps: Hang on, can you explain that part to me too?
Okay, but what does that actually mean for us?
delivery.speaker: secondary

evaluate.pass: The tech greets the second person, gives a short, plain recap of what they found, and asks for their questions or input.
evaluate.fail: The tech keeps talking only to the first person, re-explains everything at length, or pushes for a decision before the second person is caught up.

coaching.why: The person who walks in late often has an equal say, and they heard none of your explanation. If they are not caught up, the answer will be "we need to talk about it." A short recap for them is part of closing, not a delay.
coaching.modelResponse: Hi, I'm (name), nice to meet you. Here's the short version so you're caught up: I found what's causing the problem, I showed it to (partner's name), and there are a couple of ways to fix it. Before I go on, what questions do you have? I want you both to be comfortable with whatever you decide.
commonMistakes: Nodding at the second person and going on with the first
Re-explaining everything from the start at full length
Asking for the decision before the second person is caught up
Treating the second person's questions as a stall

review.author: Claude
notes: Spoken by the secondary person. Limited to the personas that define one.
Lines avoid assuming the tech's gender.

moves.name: Tests your honesty
moves.summary: The customer asks a direct question where the honest answer could cost the tech the bigger sale.

delivery.intent: Ask a direct question where the honest answer might cost the tech money, and watch how they answer. You already have a rough idea of the answer from something you read or were told, so you will notice a dodge. A straight answer, even "the cheaper one is fine for you" or "I don't know, I'll find out," raises your trust a lot. A sales pitch, a dodge, or a made-up fact lowers it a lot. Never say you are testing them.
lines: Be honest with me. Do I really need all of that?
If the cheaper fix would work, would you even tell me?
Honestly, could I get another year out of it?
Is the cheaper option actually fine, or is it junk?
followUps: Okay, but that's not really what I asked.
So is that a yes or a no?
delivery.speaker: primary

evaluate.pass: The tech answers the question directly and honestly, even when the honest answer is the cheaper choice or "I don't know, I'll find out."
evaluate.fail: The tech dodges into a sales pitch, makes up a fact to sound sure, or uses fear to steer the customer toward the more expensive option.

coaching.why: Some questions are tests. The customer often knows part of the answer already and is watching whether you tell the truth when it costs you. One honest answer that saves them money earns more trust than any pitch, and it makes the rest of your recommendations believable.
coaching.modelResponse: Honestly? Maybe. It's not leaking yet, and the burner works fine. The rust at the bottom is what I'd watch. That usually means a leak is coming, but I can't tell you when. If you want to wait, that's your call. Check the floor around it every week or so, and call us the day you see water.
commonMistakes: Answering a different question to get back to the pitch
Saying "They're both great" without answering
Making up a number or a rule to sound sure
Hinting the cheaper option is risky when it is not

review.author: Claude
notes: The honest answer depends on the scenario. Perception should compare the tech's answer with the scenario's justifiedWork, unjustifiedWork, and recommended option.

moves.name: Thinks out loud
moves.summary: After hearing the options, the customer starts weighing them out loud, stops mid-sentence, and goes quiet for a few seconds.

delivery.intent: Start weighing the options out loud, then stop in the middle of the sentence and go quiet while you think. Do not finish the thought and do not ask a question yet. If the tech waits, finish the thought yourself in one short sentence that says what you are actually weighing. If the tech jumps in, say you were still thinking.
lines: So the cheaper one fixes it for now, but if it happens again, then...
Okay. So if we went with the second one, that would mean...
[thoughtful] Hm. The longer warranty's nice, but then again, if we...
So the basic one would get us by, and then later we could maybe...
followUps: Sorry, just thinking. I'm trying to figure out if the cheaper one is really enough for us.
Hang on, I wasn't done. I was still working that out.
delivery.speaker: primary

evaluate.pass: The tech lets the unfinished thought sit for at least two and a half seconds and lets the customer finish it.
evaluate.fail: The tech finishes the customer's sentence, starts selling an option, or talks while the customer is still thinking.

coaching.why: A customer thinking out loud is making the decision in front of you. If you finish the sentence for them, you replace their reasoning with yours and they stop sharing it. If you wait, they tell you exactly what they are weighing.
coaching.modelResponse: (Stays quiet for at least three seconds and lets the customer finish.) If they stay quiet: "Take your time. What part are you weighing?" Then listens to the whole answer before saying anything about the options, and answers the part they named.
commonMistakes: Finishing the customer's sentence for them
Jumping in to sell the option they seemed to be leaning away from
Filling the pause with more details about the options
Asking "So which one?" before they finish thinking

review.author: Claude
notes: Pass and fail are measured from timing. The runtime speaks the line first, then holds the silence.
followUps[0] finishes the thought, so it also works if the runtime speaks it when the hold ends. It names a concern the tech can tie the options to. followUps[1] is for a tech who jumped in.

moves.name: I watched a video
moves.summary: The customer brings up something they learned from an online video, and it is partly or fully wrong for their situation.

delivery.intent: Bring up something you learned from an online video, with confidence. It is partly or fully wrong for your home, but you trust it, and you looked it up because you did not want to get taken. If the tech says what is right about it, corrects the rest in plain words, and does not make fun of you for looking it up, you trust them more. If they just agree, you believe the wrong thing. If they talk down to you, dig in.
lines: I watched a video on this. It's just the thermocouple, right? That's like a twenty-dollar part.
I saw a video that said if you turn the thermostat up, it heats faster.
This guy online said hard water doesn't matter with a tankless.
I saw a video that said these should last twenty-five years if you take care of them.
followUps: Well, the guy in the video seemed to know what he was talking about.
So the video was wrong?
delivery.speaker: primary

evaluate.pass: The tech says what the video got right, corrects what does not apply here in plain words, and keeps a correct recommendation.
evaluate.fail: The tech goes along with the wrong claim, mocks the video or the customer for watching it, or argues to win the point.

coaching.why: A customer who watched a video did homework so they would not get taken. If you mock it, you confirm their fear. If you agree with something wrong, you lose them when they find out. Saying what the video got right first makes the correction easy to accept.
coaching.modelResponse: Good on you for looking into it. The video's right that a thermocouple is a cheap part, and if that were all it was, I'd tell you. Here, though, the tank itself is leaking. That water soaked the burner area, which is why it won't stay lit, and a leaking tank can't be repaired. Want me to show you?
commonMistakes: Saying "You can't believe everything on the internet"
Agreeing with the video to avoid an argument
Getting technical to prove you know more
Skipping what the video got right

review.author: Claude
notes: Claims cover thermocouple cost, thermostat setting, hard water with tankless, and tank lifespan. The thermostat, hard water, and lifespan claims are wrong; the thermocouple claim is partly right.
When the claim is right for this job (for example the thermocouple in wh-repair-or-replace-9yr), honest_answer passes. The tech should say so.

moves.name: Would you do this in your own house?
moves.summary: The customer asks what the tech would do if it were their own house and their own money.

delivery.intent: Ask what the tech would do if it were their own house and their own money. You want a real answer, not a pitch. If they answer honestly, with a reason that fits your situation, trust them more, even if the answer is the cheaper option. If they name the most expensive option with no reason tied to you, or just say "it's up to you," trust them less and press once.
lines: Would you do this in your own house?
Be honest. If this was your house, what would you do?
What would you pick, if it was your money?
If your mom had this problem, what would you tell her to do?
followUps: But what would you actually do? Not the sales answer.
Okay, but would you pay that much for it?
delivery.speaker: primary

evaluate.pass: The tech says what they would actually do and why, based on this home and what the customer told them, even if it is not the most expensive option.
evaluate.fail: The tech dodges, names the most expensive option with no reason that fits this customer, makes up a story, or uses the question to push for a decision now.

coaching.why: This question is the customer asking whether they can trust you. A real answer, with a reason that fits their home, often decides the sale. A dodge or an automatic "the best one" tells them your recommendation is about your paycheck.
coaching.modelResponse: Honestly? If it were my house, I'd go with the standard tank and the code upgrades. It's reliable, and the warranty covers what usually goes wrong. The tankless is a good unit, but for two people it would take a long time to make back the extra cost. If it were my money, I'd keep that difference.
commonMistakes: Saying "It's totally up to you" without answering
Naming the most expensive option with no reason tied to them
Making up a personal story to sound relatable
Following the answer with "So should we get started?" right away

review.author: Claude
notes: Pairs with drill your-own-house.
The model response fits a two-person household choosing between a standard tank and tankless. The honest answer changes with the scenario.

scenarios.title: Kitchen sink keeps clogging
scenarios.briefing: Service call. Kitchen sink backed up this morning with standing water in both sides. Customer says it is the third clog this year. Two-story home on a slab. Not a member.
scenarios.situation: The 2-inch ABS kitchen drain clogs every two to three months because grease and food paste coat the inside of the pipe. The tech opens the line with a small cable through the cleanout behind the trap so the sinks drain, then runs a camera to see why it keeps coming back. A cable punches a path through the buildup and the sink drains again, but the coating stays on the walls and the line closes up within weeks. That is what happened after the last two clearings (one by another company in the spring, one with a store-bought snake in the summer). The pipe itself is sound: no cracks, no roots, no low spots. Hydro jetting scours the pipe wall back to full size, and a camera pass afterward proves it. Jetting is the honest recommendation because the history and the footage both show buildup along the whole run, not a single blockage. Replacing or relining the line is not justified. The customer works from home with two kids under six and wants one clear recommendation she can trust, quickly.

equipment.item: 2-inch ABS kitchen drain, about 32 feet to the main
equipment.notes: Cleanout tee behind the trap. Pipe sound, heavily coated with grease.
Works normally. Used several times a day.

findings.text: The camera shows a thick layer of grease and food paste on the pipe walls for most of the 32 feet to the main. In places the opening is down to about half the pipe.
The cable opened a path through the clog, but the coating is still on the walls. That is why the last two clearings only lasted a few weeks.
The pipe has no cracks, roots, or low spots. The problem is buildup, not damage.
Cooking grease and starchy scraps like rice, pasta, and potato peels go down the disposal most days. That feeds the buildup.

justifiedWork.label: Hydro jet the kitchen line
justifiedWork.rationale: Three clogs this year and camera footage of grease along the whole run. Jetting removes the coating. A cable only opens a path through it.

justifiedWork.label: Camera the line after jetting
justifiedWork.rationale: Confirms the pipe is clean and sound, and gives the customer video of the result.

justifiedWork.label: Explain what to keep out of the disposal
justifiedWork.rationale: Grease and starchy scraps cause the buildup. Without a change the line will coat again.

unjustifiedWork.label: Replacing or relining the kitchen drain
unjustifiedWork.why: The camera shows sound pipe with no cracks, roots, or sags. Jetting removes the buildup.

unjustifiedWork.label: Replacing the garbage disposal
unjustifiedWork.why: The disposal works normally. How it is used, not the unit, causes the buildup.

unjustifiedWork.label: Jetting the main sewer line
unjustifiedWork.why: Every other drain in the house runs freely. Nothing points to a main line problem.

options.label: Cable clearing only
includes: Kitchen line opened with a cable machine today
Camera look to find the cause
Both sinks and the disposal tested
The grease coating stays on the pipe walls

options.label: Hydro jet and camera
includes: Hydro jet the full kitchen line to the main
Camera video of the clean line sent to you
A short list of what to keep out of the disposal

scenarios.goal: Use the camera footage to explain why the clog keeps coming back, recommend jetting as one clear choice with the cable option shown honestly, and ask for a decision without pressure.

review.author: Claude
notes: Prices are placeholders inside public Riverside County ranges; each company's price book replaces them.
Assumes the camera look on a repeat clog is part of the cable price. Adjust if the company charges it separately.

scenarios.title: Main line backup, roots in a clay sewer
scenarios.briefing: Service call. Toilets and the hall tub are backing up, and sewage came up in the shower drain this morning. Single-story home built in 1968. Exterior cleanout by the front hose bib. Not a member.
scenarios.situation: The 4-inch clay sewer lateral is blocked by tree roots. The tech clears it with a cable and root-cutting head through the front cleanout, and the house drains again. The camera then shows roots entering at two joints about 38 and 44 feet out, under the front lawn near a mature Modesto ash, and the joint at 44 feet is offset and cracked. The rest of the clay line, from the house to 35 feet and from 47 feet to the city sewer at about 70 feet, has tight joints with no roots or sags. Clearing restores flow today, but roots grow back through open joints, usually within six to eighteen months. A spot repair that replaces about 10 feet of clay with PVC at the damaged joints is the honest recommendation. It fixes the cause, and the rest of the line does not need work. Lining the whole line is a real option but not needed based on the footage. Carlos wants the cheapest fix and brings up his brother-in-law, who is a plumber. Elena wants it done right once. Money is tight after a car repair.

equipment.item: 4-inch clay sewer lateral, about 70 feet to the city sewer
equipment.notes: Roots at two joints near the ash tree. One joint offset and cracked. Rest of the line sound.

equipment.item: Exterior sewer cleanout at the front of the house
equipment.notes: Good access for clearing and camera work.

findings.text: Roots are growing into the line at two joints about 38 and 44 feet from the cleanout, under the front lawn near the ash tree. They caused today's backup.
The joint at 44 feet is offset about half an inch and cracked. Roots and soil get in there, and no amount of clearing closes it.
The rest of the clay line has tight joints with no roots, cracks, or sags, from the house to 35 feet and from 47 feet to the city connection.
The line is clear and draining after the root cutting. The house is usable today.

justifiedWork.label: Clear the line with a root cutter
justifiedWork.rationale: The house was backing up. Clearing restores use today.

justifiedWork.label: Replace about 10 feet of clay with PVC at the root-damaged joints
justifiedWork.rationale: Removes the open, cracked joints where roots get in. The camera shows the rest of the line is sound.

justifiedWork.label: Camera the line after the repair
justifiedWork.rationale: Confirms the new section and both connections are clean and sloped correctly.

justifiedWork.label: Permit and inspection for the sewer repair
justifiedWork.rationale: Sewer line repairs require a permit and inspection.

unjustifiedWork.label: Saying the whole line must be lined
unjustifiedWork.why: The camera shows tight, root-free joints on both sides of the damaged section. Lining is a choice, not a need.

unjustifiedWork.label: Digging up and replacing the entire lateral
unjustifiedWork.why: Only one 10-foot section is damaged. Excavating 70 feet of yard is not justified.

unjustifiedWork.label: Replacing the drain lines inside the house
unjustifiedWork.why: The backup came from roots in the yard. Every interior drain ran clear once the lateral was open.

options.label: Root clearing only
includes: Cable and root-cutter clearing done today
Camera video of the full line
Roots will grow back, usually within 6 to 18 months

options.label: Spot repair of the root section
includes: Excavate and replace about 10 feet of clay with PVC

options.label: Trenchless lining of the full lateral
includes: Hydro jet the line to prepare it for lining
Epoxy liner from the cleanout to the city connection
Permit and camera video after lining

scenarios.goal: Show the footage so both Carlos and Elena understand why the line backed up, and present clearing, spot repair, and lining honestly. Recommend the spot repair, handle the brother-in-law without arguing, and help them decide together.

review.author: Claude
notes: Prices are placeholders inside public Riverside County ranges; each company's price book replaces them.
Spot repair price assumes about 4 feet of depth in a lawn with no concrete to cut.
Verify local permit rules and whether the city owns any part of the lateral in the public right of way.

scenarios.title: Bathroom sink clog, simple clear
scenarios.briefing: Service call. Hall bathroom sink has been draining slowly for weeks and stopped completely last night. Single-story home built in 1979. Not a member.
scenarios.situation: A simple clog. Hair and soap scum are packed around the pop-up stopper and in the trap. The tech pulls and cleans the stopper and runs a hand cable through the trap and the short branch line, and the sink drains at full speed. Every other drain in the house (tub, both toilets, kitchen, laundry) runs freely, so there is no main line or vent problem. The honest work is the simple clear, done today at the lowest price. The stopper is old and sticks, so replacing the pop-up assembly is a small, optional add-on. Hydro jetting or a camera inspection is not justified. The company membership can be mentioned once, briefly, as optional, and she should never feel the repair depends on it. She lives on a fixed income and has been sold work she did not need before.

equipment.item: Bathroom sink pop-up drain assembly, chrome
equipment.notes: Stopper sticks and does not seal well. No leaks.

equipment.item: Hall bathroom sink trap and branch line
equipment.notes: Packed with hair and soap scum. Pipe in good condition.

findings.text: Hair and soap scum are packed around the stopper and in the trap. That is the whole clog.
The tub, both toilets, the kitchen, and the laundry all drain normally. Nothing points to a problem further down the line.
The pop-up stopper sticks and does not seal well. It still works. Replacing it is optional.
After the clearing, a full basin drains in a few seconds.

justifiedWork.label: Clean the stopper and clear the trap and branch with a hand cable
justifiedWork.rationale: This removes the whole clog. The sink drains normally afterward.

justifiedWork.label: Test with a full basin and check the other drains
justifiedWork.rationale: Confirms the clog is gone and the rest of the system drains.

justifiedWork.label: Show her how to keep hair out of the drain
justifiedWork.rationale: A simple strainer and cleaning the stopper every few months prevent the next clog.

unjustifiedWork.label: Hydro jetting the drain lines
unjustifiedWork.why: One hair clog at the stopper, and every other drain runs freely. Jetting is not needed.

unjustifiedWork.label: Camera inspection of the drain or sewer
unjustifiedWork.why: Nothing points to a problem past the trap. A camera would not change the repair.

unjustifiedWork.label: Cleaning the main sewer line
unjustifiedWork.why: The main is not involved. All other fixtures drain normally.

scenarios.title: Drinking water filter question, in Spanish
scenarios.briefing: Customer asked about a filter for drinking water. She speaks Spanish at home and some English; this call is in Spanish. Single-story home. Not a member.
scenarios.situation: The customer buys bottled water, about $40 a month in 5-gallon jugs, because she does not like the taste of the tap water and is not sure it is safe. The water district's annual report shows the tap water meets state and federal drinking water standards. A TDS meter at the kitchen tap reads about 540 parts per million. That measures dissolved minerals; it is not a safety test, and an honest tech says so. A simple under-sink reverse osmosis system is the honest recommendation. It improves taste, removes most dissolved minerals and many contaminants such as lead and arsenic, and replaces the bottled water. It does not treat shower or laundry water, it sends some water down the drain while it filters, and its filters need changing on a schedule, about $120 a year. A whole-house system or a UV light is not justified on city water. She usually has her daughter help with decisions like this and is careful about agreeing to something she cannot fully check.

scenarios.title: Gas smell at the water heater
scenarios.briefing: Same-day call. Customer reports a faint gas smell in the garage near the water heater since this morning. 40-gallon gas tank in the garage. Not a member.
scenarios.situation: The gas connector to the water heater is leaking. It is an old uncoated brass connector that was reused at the last install. It is corroded at the lower fitting and kinked behind the tank, and leak solution bubbles at that fitting. The gas shutoff valve for the water heater is an old plug valve. It is stiff and shows a small bubble at the stem when it is turned. It closed and held, but it is not reliable. There is no sediment trap. With the water heater valve closed, the meter shows no other leak, and the other gas appliances test tight. The smell was faint and limited to the water heater area. It was not a strong smell, which would mean leaving the house and calling the gas company. Safety comes first. The tech confirms the leak, shuts off the gas to the water heater, airs out the garage, and tells the customer calmly that it is safe now and what happens next. The water heater stays off until it is fixed. The honest recommendation is to replace the connector and the shutoff valve, add a sediment trap, leak test, relight, and check the draft, today. The tank is 14 years old with light rust at the base but no leak and a good burner, so replacement is a fair option to mention because of its age, not because of the gas leak. Calm, honest urgency passes. Scare talk, worst-case stories, or saying the tank must be replaced for safety fails.

scenarios.title: Scale buildup and the softener question

Nothing is damaged yet: no leaks, no failed fixtures, and the water heater works normally. The builder put a softener loop with a bypass in the garage, so a standard softener is a simple install. scenarios.title: Member tune-up finds a worn anode
scenarios.briefing: Membership tune-up. The customer is a member. Annual water heater service with a flush, relief valve test, and burner check. 50-gallon gas tank in the garage, about 6 years old. No complaints reported.
scenarios.situation: This is the customer's included yearly tune-up. During the service the tech pulls the anode rod and finds it used up. Most of it is bare steel core wire with only a few pieces of magnesium left. The anode corrodes in place of the tank steel, and once it is gone the tank starts to rust from the inside. The tank is sound. There are no leaks and no rust at the base or the fittings, the burner and draft are good, and the flush brought out a normal amount of sediment for the hard water here. The expansion tank holds air, and its pressure was set to match the house. The honest recommendation is a new anode rod, not a new tank. The ceiling is low, so a flexible link-style anode is needed. A new anode can add years to a sound tank, but there is no guarantee, and the tech should not promise a number. The tank's 6-year manufacturer warranty is at or near its end. If the customer brings up a home warranty, most plans treat an anode as maintenance, but the tech should not guess about the customer's contract and can offer to look at it together. Member pricing applies.

scenarios.title: 110 psi and a failing pressure regulator
scenarios.briefing: Service call. Customer says the relief valve on the water heater drips and the pipes bang when the washer shuts off. He asked for a quote to replace the water heater. Two-story home built in 2001. Not a member.
scenarios.situation: The water heater is fine. Static pressure at the hose bib reads 110 psi. Code requires a pressure regulator when static pressure is over 80 psi, and most homes are set between 50 and 70. The original 25-year-old regulator at the front of the house has failed, and turning its adjusting screw does not change the reading. The high pressure makes the relief valve on the 6-year-old water heater open and drip, causes the banging, and makes the toilet fill valves hiss. The honest fix is a new regulator set to about 60 psi, then resetting the expansion tank's air charge and rechecking the relief valve once pressure is down. The customer read online that a dripping relief valve means the water heater is failing, and he is confident about it. Replacing the water heater is not justified.

scenarios.title: 1960s galvanized pipe, low water pressure
scenarios.briefing: Service call. Low water pressure throughout the house, worst at the back bathroom, and rusty water after the water has sat overnight. Single-story home on a raised foundation, built in 1962. Not a member.

scenarios.title: Sewer camera before selling finds a belly
scenarios.briefing: Scheduled sewer camera inspection. Homeowner plans to sell in a couple of years and wants to know the condition of the line before a buyer's inspector does. Single-story home built in 1987. No backups reported.
scenarios.situation: The tech runs the camera from the exterior cleanout to the city sewer, about 62 feet. The 4-inch ABS line has a belly, a sag where the soil settled, from about 34 to 41 feet. The low spot holds about an inch and a half of water, and toilet paper is collecting at its downstream end. There are no roots, cracks, or separated joints, and the house has never backed up. California sellers disclose known defects; the law does not require this repair before a sale, and disclosure questions belong with his agent. He does not want to put money into a house he will not enjoy.

scenarios.title: High water bill, hot line leaking under the slab
scenarios.briefing: Leak detection call. Water bill jumped from about $90 to $260 in one billing cycle, and the customer hears water running when everything is off. Single-story home on a slab, built in 1977. Not a member.
scenarios.situation: The hot water line under the slab has a pinhole leak. With every fixture off, the meter's leak indicator turns steadily. Closing the cold inlet valve at the water heater stops it, which puts the leak on the hot side. A pressure test shows the cold side holds with no drop. Acoustic listening finds the loudest point under the hallway tile about 6 feet from the hall bathroom, and a thermal camera shows a warm patch in the same spot. The home has its original soft copper lines under the slab. A spot repair means breaking through the hallway tile and concrete. It fixes this leak, but the same 49-year-old hot line can leak somewhere else later, and tile replacement is extra. Rerouting the hot line through the attic with PEX takes the hot water out of the slab for good and leaves the floor alone. The reroute is the honest recommendation for this home, with the spot repair shown as a fair lower-cost choice. A whole-house repipe is not justified. The customer works night shifts as an ER nurse and was overcharged by another company, so she will want to see the proof at every step.

scenarios.title: Family of five, tank or tankless
scenarios.briefing: Estimate. Homeowners report the water heater is leaking and the family runs out of hot water most mornings. They want to compare a tank and a tankless unit. 40-gallon gas tank in the garage. Not a member.
scenarios.situation: The 11-year-old 40-gallon gas tank is leaking at the base and has to be replaced. It was also too small for a family of five, which is why the hot water runs out on busy mornings. There is no expansion tank and the house has a pressure regulator. The gas line can supply a high-recovery tank, but a 199,000 BTU tankless would need a larger line from the meter, new PVC venting, and an outlet. The water is hard, so a tankless unit here would need descaling about once a year. There are three honest options. The same 40-gallon size is the cheapest but will not fix the running out. A 50-gallon high-recovery tank (about 65,000 BTU, with a first-hour rating around 90 gallons compared with about 70 for the old tank) covers the family's morning use for about half the price of tankless. A tankless unit gives endless hot water and a longer life but costs the most up front and needs yearly descaling. The honest recommendation is the 50-gallon high-recovery tank, because it solves the problem the family called about without overspending. Tankless is a fair choice if they value endless hot water and plan to stay a long time. The two spouses may want different things, and the tech should learn what each one cares about and tie the options to both.

scenarios.title: Rumbling 8-year tank, flush or replace
scenarios.briefing: Service call. Customer reports loud rumbling and popping from the water heater when it heats. 50-gallon gas tank in the garage, about 8 years old. Not a member.
scenarios.situation: The rumbling is sediment. The water here is hard, and minerals settle at the bottom of the tank. Water trapped under that layer turns to steam when the burner fires, which makes the popping. It is not dangerous by itself, but it wastes gas and overheats the bottom of the tank, which shortens its life. The 8-year-old 50-gallon gas tank has no leaks and no rust at the base or the fittings. The burner, draft, and relief valve are good, the anode rod is about half used, which is normal for its age, and the expansion tank holds air. The honest recommendation is a flush and service with a new brass drain valve, because the plastic one is likely to clog or leak during a first flush. The tech should set expectations. Hardened sediment may not all come out, so the noise may get quieter rather than stop, and there is a small chance a tank this age shows a leak after its first flush. Replacement is not needed today. At 8 years it is honest to suggest budgeting for one in the next few years.

scenarios.title: Failing electric tank, heat pump option
scenarios.briefing: Estimate. Homeowner reports lukewarm water and a small puddle under the water heater, and wants to discuss heat pump water heaters. 50-gallon electric tank in the garage. All-electric home. Not a member.
scenarios.situation: The 13-year-old 50-gallon electric tank is failing. Water is seeping from the bottom of the tank, and the lower heating element reads open, which is why the water is lukewarm. The tank cannot be repaired. There is no expansion tank, and the house has a pressure regulator, so the new install needs one. The home suits a heat pump water heater. The existing 240-volt, 30-amp circuit can serve a 240-volt unit (confirm against the model's nameplate). The two-car garage has far more air than the roughly 700 cubic feet many units call for, there is a route for a condensate drain to the outside, and the garage stays inside the heat pump's operating range most of the year. Accurate numbers: a standard electric tank is rated at a UEF of about 0.92 and a 50-gallon heat pump unit at about 3.5 to 4, so it uses roughly a quarter to a third of the electricity for the same hot water. In hybrid mode its first-hour rating is about the same as the old tank's. It runs at roughly 45 to 55 decibels, about like a dehumidifier, cools and dries the air around it, and recovers more slowly in heat pump only mode. Payback depends on the home's usage and electric rate, and the tech should work it out from the customer's bill, not promise a number. Rebates may apply, verify current amounts. Incentives for heat pump water heaters have come from TECH Clean California, local utility programs, and the federal tax credit, and funding and eligibility change often. The federal 25C credit ended for equipment placed in service after December 31, 2025. A like-for-like electric replacement is allowed in an existing home, so the heat pump is a choice, not a code requirement. The honest recommendation is the 50-gallon heat pump unit, presented with accurate numbers and without overstating savings or rebates.

scenarios.title: 9-year tank, failed thermocouple
scenarios.briefing: Service call. Homeowner reports no hot water and says the pilot keeps going out. 40-gallon gas tank in the garage, about 9 years old. Not a member.
scenarios.situation: The thermocouple has failed. The pilot lights, but it goes out when the control knob is released, and the thermocouple tests low on a millivolt meter, below what it takes to hold the gas valve open. On this sealed-burner tank the thermocouple comes as a pilot assembly with the igniter, and replacing it is a routine repair. The air intake screen at the base of the tank is coated with lint and dust, which can starve the burner of air, so it should be cleaned. The tank is sound. There are no leaks and no rust at the base or the fittings, and the gas control valve works. The honest recommendation is the repair. Tanks in this area usually last 8 to 12 years with the hard water here, so at 9 years this tank has some life left. The honest thing is to say that plainly and suggest planning for a replacement, not to do one today. A tech who pushes replacement, or blames the gas control valve to sell a bigger repair, fails the integrity test. A flush should not be added to this repair, because on a 9-year tank that has never been flushed it can make the drain valve leak.

There are no leaks and no rust at the base or the fittings. The tank is sound.
The gas control valve works and holds. It does not need to be replaced.

scenarios.title: Tankless error code, descale needed
scenarios.briefing: Service call. Customer reports the tankless water heater shuts off in the middle of showers and shows an error code. Gas tankless unit on the garage wall, about 6 years old. Customer wants it fixed today. Not a member.
scenarios.situation: The 6-year-old condensing gas tankless is showing its scale warning code. It has never been descaled, and with the hard water here scale has built up in the heat exchanger, which makes it overheat and shut down during longer showers. The cold inlet filter screen is also partly clogged with scale. Isolation valves with flush ports were installed with the unit, so a descale can be done today in about an hour to an hour and a half. Gas pressure holds within spec at full fire, and the vent and condensate lines are clear. The honest fix is a descale and service. Because the water is hard, the unit will need descaling about once a year, which is a fair reason to offer the membership if it includes that service. An inline scale-reduction cartridge is a reasonable optional add, not a requirement. Nothing found justifies replacing the unit, upgrading the gas line, or adding a recirculation pump. The customer wants a quick answer and a price. A strong tech gives a short diagnosis, says the price clearly, and gets it done.

scenarios.title: Tank replacement, customer asks about tankless
scenarios.briefing: Estimate. Homeowner reports a small puddle under the water heater and has been reading about tankless water heaters. 50-gallon gas tank in the garage of a two-story house. Not a member.
scenarios.situation: The 11-year-old 50-gallon gas tank has rust at the base and a slow seep from under the jacket. It still makes hot water, but it is at the end of its life and should be replaced. The household has never run out of hot water with it. There is no expansion tank, and the house has a pressure regulator, so the new install needs one. The customer asks about tankless and believes some claims that are partly wrong: that it pays for itself in a couple of years, that it gives instant hot water at the tap, that it needs no maintenance, and that it can run on the existing gas line. The facts for this house: a 199,000 BTU tankless needs a larger gas line from the meter (the line to the water heater is 1/2 inch), and the gas company may need to set a larger meter. It needs new PVC venting through the wall and a 120-volt outlet. With the hard water here it needs descaling about once a year. It does not get hot water to the tap any faster without a recirculation system, and it will not run during a power outage. Its real advantages are endless hot water, a longer service life, and lower gas use, but at this household's usage the extra cost takes many years to pay back. The honest recommendation is the 50-gallon tank. Tankless is a fair choice if the customer still wants it after hearing the facts, and the tech should respect that choice.

drills.title: The first 30 seconds at the door
drills.why: In the first thirty seconds at the door, the customer decides how much to trust you. Most techs say a quick hello, ask where the water heater is, and walk right past the person who called. Others talk about the company for a full minute. Either way, the customer is left with questions nobody answered. How long will this take? What will it cost? Am I going to get talked into something? Think about what this is like for them. A stranger is about to walk through their house, and they're worried about money before you've said a word. So answer those questions first. Say your name, your company, and their name. Tell them how the visit will go: a few questions, a look at the problem, then you'll show them what you found and go over options and prices before any work starts. Say about how long it takes. In this drill, Margaret opens the door. Tell her how the visit will go.

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: Hi, you must be Margaret. I'm Chris, the plumber you called about your hot water.

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: Oh, hello. Come in, please. It's been out since yesterday morning.

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: Sorry, that's a long time to go without. Here's how this goes. I'll ask a few questions, then look at the heater. About twenty minutes.

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: Oh. All right. That's not so bad.

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: Then I'll show you what I found and your options, with prices. Nothing gets done until you decide. Where's the heater?

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: Well, that's a relief. It's out in the garage, through here.

Explain the steps of the visit and about how long it takes
Say she will see what you find, her options, and prices before any work starts
