drills.title: Five discovery questions
drills.why: This moment happens before you touch the equipment. It's the short conversation where you learn about the person, not just the problem. Most techs ask one question, something like "So what's going on?", and head straight for the heater. Or they only ask questions with yes or no answers. Then, when it's time for options, they're guessing what this customer cares about. The facts that matter most in this call are not in the garage. Who lives here. How long they plan to stay. What happened the last time they hired someone. What they're worried about. Customers will tell you all of it if you ask, and they trust you more for asking. So ask five open questions, two about the problem and three about them. Listen to the whole answer. Follow up on one thing they say. Then say back what you heard before you start working. In this drill, you're in the garage with Margaret. Ask your five questions first.

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: Before I look at it, can I ask you a few things? Tell me what happened when it stopped working.

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: Well, yesterday morning the shower just went cold. And there was water on the garage floor.

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: That helps. Who lives here with you, and how do you use hot water on a normal day?

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: Oh, it's just me now. My husband Harold passed four years ago. He always handled these things.

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: I'm sorry. So you're taking care of the house on your own now. What matters most to you in how we fix this?

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: Well, I don't want to spend more than I have to. And I don't want to be fooled again.

drills.priorContext: The tech introduced themselves at the front door and explained how the visit will go. Margaret has led the tech into the garage, where the 40-gallon gas water heater sits next to the washer. There is some water on the floor around its base. The tech has not inspected the heater yet and has not asked her any questions beyond confirming she has had no hot water since yesterday morning.
drills.techPrompt: Before you look at the heater, ask Margaret five open questions, two about the problem and three about her.
passCriteria: Ask at least five questions, most of them open-ended
Ask at least two about her (who lives here, her plans, what matters to her), not the equipment
Follow up on at least one of her answers
Say back what you heard before you move on

review.author: Claude
notes: No customerOpener, so the tech speaks first.
The last demo line hints at her roof coating regret, which the persona reveals at trust 50 on previous-work or history topics.

drills.title: Explaining a finding in plain language
drills.why: You've found the problem. Now explain it so the customer understands it. Most techs explain it the way they would to another tech. The anode's gone, the tank's rusted through, the combustion chamber's soaked. Or they just say it's shot. The customer nods along, understands almost none of it, and now has to make a big decision based on trust alone. Here's what is going on for them. When people don't understand, most don't ask. They get quiet, and then they get suspicious. If they can't explain it to a family member that night, the answer will be that they need to think about it. So explain it in three parts, in everyday words. What's wrong. Why it happened. What it means for them. If you have to use a trade word, explain it in the same sentence. Then ask if it makes sense. In this drill, Margaret asks what you found. Explain it so she could repeat it to her son.

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: Well? Is it bad news? Can you fix it?

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: I wish I could. The tank itself is leaking from the bottom. After twelve years, the steel inside rusts through, and that's where your water is coming from.

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: Oh dear. Can't you patch it somehow?

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: Not in a way that would last. And the water soaked the spot where the burner lights, so it won't stay on. That's why you have no hot water. Does that make sense?

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: I think so. So it has to be replaced, then.

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: It does. What questions do you have before we talk about your choices?

drills.priorContext: The tech introduced themselves, asked Margaret about the water heater and her household, and then spent about fifteen minutes inspecting the heater in the garage while she waited in the kitchen. The tech has not told her anything about what they found yet. She saw water on the garage floor yesterday and is hoping it is something simple. She has come to the garage door to hear the news.
drills.customerOpener: You were out there a while. Is it bad news? Can you fix it?
drills.techPrompt: Margaret asks what you found. In plain words, tell her what's wrong, why it happened, and what it means for her.
passCriteria: Explain what is wrong, why it happened, and what it means for her
Use no trade terms without explaining them in the same sentence
Check that it made sense before you talk about options or price

review.author: Claude
notes: Starts in findings, so the engine adds the mid-call trust and understanding bonus. If the tech uses jargon, understanding drops and Margaret asks what it means.

drills.title: Showing what you found
drills.why: This moment is about letting the customer see the problem. Most techs tell instead of show. When the customer says, "I'll take your word for it," they're glad to skip it. Then the price comes, and all they have is your word. Here's what is really going on. Many homeowners have paid for work they didn't need. When someone says they wouldn't know what they're looking at, they aren't saying they don't care. They're unsure, and a little embarrassed. Seeing the rust and the water for themselves answers the question they won't ask out loud: is this real? So make it easy to say yes. Tell them it takes a minute, they don't need to know anything, and you'll point. Show them one or two things and say what each one means. If they still say no, show them a photo on your phone. In this drill, Margaret says she doesn't need to see it. Make it easy for her to look.

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: Oh, you don't need to show me. I wouldn't know what I'm looking at anyway.

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: You don't need to know a thing. It's right inside the garage door, and I'll point. It takes a minute.

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: Well... all right, if you think I should.

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: See the rust around the bottom, and the water under it? That's coming out of the tank itself. That's why it can't be repaired.

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: Oh my. I had no idea it looked like that.

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: I took photos too, so you'll have them with the estimate. What questions do you have?

drills.priorContext: The tech has inspected the 12-year-old gas water heater in the garage and told Margaret in one sentence that the tank is leaking and will need to be replaced. Margaret is standing in the kitchen doorway. She has not seen the leak up close. She feels a little foolish about not understanding these things, because her late husband Harold always handled them.
drills.customerOpener: Oh, you don't need to show me. I wouldn't know what I'm looking at anyway.
drills.techPrompt: Margaret says she doesn't need to see it. Make it easy for her to look, then show her the leak.
passCriteria: Offer again in a way that is easy to accept, and use a photo if she still says no
Point to the leak and the rust and say what each one means in plain words
Ask what questions she has before moving on

review.author: Claude
notes: The opener is the moment itself. No move is forced, so nothing repeats it.
If Margaret declines a second time, a photo on the phone should pass. Pressing a third time should not.

drills.title: Three options tied to what they told you
drills.why: This is the moment you present the customer's choices. Most techs get it wrong in one of two ways. Some give one option and nothing else. Others read three options off the tablet, cheapest to most expensive, with the same speech they give everyone. Either way, the customer can't tell which choice fits them. Here's what the customer wants at this point. They want a real choice, and they want to know which one you would pick for them. Options only mean something when they're tied to what the customer told you. So think back to discovery. Give each option in a sentence or two, and connect it to something they said: who lives there, how long they're staying, what worries them. Be honest about who each option is not for. Then recommend one, the honest best fit, and give the reason in their words. In this drill, Margaret asks about her choices. Give her three, and recommend one.

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: Well, I suppose if it has to be replaced, what are my choices?

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: There are three. The first is a standard tank like the one you have, with a six-year warranty. For one person who plans to stay, it does the job well.

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: And what about the other two?

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: The second is the same size with a ten-year warranty, and it heats back up faster. The third is tankless. It never runs out, but for one shower a day, you'd be paying for more than you need.

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: Oh my. So which one makes the most sense for me?

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: The standard one. You told me you want something reliable without spending more than you have to. That's the one that fits.

drills.priorContext: Earlier in the visit Margaret told the tech that she has lived alone since her husband Harold passed, that she takes one shower a day and does a couple of loads of laundry a week, and that she plans to stay in the house as long as she can. She also said she does not want to spend more than she has to. The tech showed her the leak at the base of the 12-year-old tank and explained that it cannot be repaired. She understands it needs to be replaced. No options or prices have been mentioned yet.
drills.customerOpener: Well, I suppose if it has to be replaced, what are my choices?
drills.techPrompt: Present the three options. Tie each one to something Margaret told you, and recommend the one that fits her best.
passCriteria: Present all three options as real choices, each in a sentence or two
Connect at least two of them to something Margaret said
Recommend one option with a reason that fits her
Do not describe tankless or the premium option as required

review.author: Claude
notes: The engine starts options with optionsPresented set to 2. That only matters for scope objections, and Margaret has none.
If the tech states prices here, the phase moves to price and silence-after-price can fire. That is fine.

drills.title: Saying the price without flinching
drills.why: This is the moment you say the number. Most techs soften the price without noticing. They start with "unfortunately." They say, "I know it's a lot, but." They give a range, or say "somewhere around," or put the number in the middle of a long explanation. Some offer a discount before the customer has said a word. Here's what the customer hears. They're paying attention to how you say the price as much as the price itself. If you sound unsure, they assume the number is padded, or that it will come down if they push. If you say it plainly, they believe it's the real price. This is harder when the customer is nervous, because their nerves make you nervous. So say what's included in one sentence, then the exact total. No range, no apology. Use the voice you'd use to tell someone the time. Then stop. In this drill, Margaret is nervous to hear it. Tell her the price.

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: Oh dear. I'm almost afraid to ask. How much is the one you'd recommend?

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: For the standard heater, with the expansion tank and earthquake straps the code requires, the permit, and hauling the old one away, it's eighteen ninety.

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: Eighteen ninety. Is that everything, or does more get added on later?

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: That's everything. Eighteen ninety is the whole job, and it's the number you'll see in writing.

drills.priorContext: The tech showed Margaret the leak, explained why the 12-year-old tank has to be replaced, and presented three options. The tech recommended the standard 40-gallon gas heater with a 6-year warranty because she lives alone and plans to stay in the house, and she agreed it sounds right for her. She has not heard any prices yet and is nervous about what it will cost.
drills.customerOpener: Oh dear. I'm almost afraid to ask. How much is the one you'd recommend?
drills.techPrompt: Margaret is nervous to hear it. Tell her the standard option's total, $1,890, and what it includes. Then stop.
passCriteria: Say the exact total once, with no range, apology, or "unfortunately"
Say in one sentence what the price includes
Offer no discount and no financing before she reacts
If she repeats the number back, confirm it calmly without lowering it

review.author: Claude
notes: Margaret weights silence-after-price at 3, so she will almost always go quiet after the number. The drill judges how the price is said, and hold-the-silence (order 7) covers the wait.

drills.title: The silence after price
drills.why: Here is the moment that costs techs more money than any other. You say the price, and the customer goes quiet. Most people can't stand that quiet. Within two or three seconds they start talking: explaining the price, apologizing for it, offering financing, or worse, knocking a hundred dollars off. Every one of those tells the customer the number was soft. Here is what is really happening in that silence. The customer is doing math. They are thinking about their budget, their week, what their spouse will say. They are not rejecting you. The silence belongs to them. Your job is to say the price clearly, once, and then wait. Count to five in your head if you have to. Let them speak first. When they do, you will learn exactly what they are worried about, and that is the conversation you actually need to have. In this drill, you will say the price, and the customer will go quiet. Hold it.

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: For the standard option, everything included, it comes to eighteen ninety.

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: (six seconds of silence) Hm. That's more than I was hoping.

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: I understand. What were you hoping it would be closer to?

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: Well, I don't know. I'm on a fixed income, you see.

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: Thank you for telling me. Let's look at what fits. Would a monthly number help?

drills.priorContext: The tech has already introduced themselves, asked about the water heater's history, shown Margaret the leak at the base of the tank, and explained in plain words why it has to be replaced. Margaret understands and is waiting to hear the price for the standard option.
drills.customerOpener: All right. So what is this going to cost me?
drills.techPrompt: Say the price for the standard option, $1,890, then stop talking.
passCriteria: State the price once, clearly, without apologizing
Wait at least four seconds before speaking again
When the customer speaks, ask about their reaction before defending the price

review.author: Claude
notes: Gold example drill.

drills.title: "I need three bids"
drills.why: Every tech hears this one: "I always get three bids." Most techs answer in a way that makes the customer want to shop even more. They drop the price to keep the job. They warn that other companies do sloppy work. Or they push for a decision now. Here's what is really going on. Three bids is almost never about the number three. It's about feeling sure the price is fair. Most homeowners don't know what a proper install includes, so they compare totals, and a lower total looks better even when it leaves out things the job requires. So respect the choice. Ask what they want to learn from the other bids. Make your estimate easy to compare: in writing, line by line. If they already have another quote, go through it together, point out anything it doesn't list, and suggest they ask that company. Never criticize the other company. In this drill, Devin has a lower quote and wants one more. Help him compare.

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: I appreciate it. But I always get three bids before I do anything like this.

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: That makes sense. Can I ask what you'll be comparing? Mostly the total, or what's included?

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: Mostly the total. The other quote was fourteen fifty. Yours is twenty-one fifty.

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: Let's put them side by side. Mine lists the expansion tank, the permit, and haul-away. Theirs doesn't mention them, so ask them if those are included.

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: Huh. Okay, that's fair. I didn't even think to check that.

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: Here's mine in writing, line by line. Get your third bid, and if you have questions about any of them, call me.

drills.priorContext: The tech showed Devin the seep and rust at the base of his 10-year-old 50-gallon gas tank and explained that it needs to be replaced. The tech recommended the standard 50-gallon option at $2,150, which includes the expansion tank the pressure regulator makes necessary, two seismic straps, a new gas connector, the permit, and haul-away, and handed Devin an itemized estimate. Devin already has a written quote from another company for $1,450 that says only "50-gallon gas water heater, installed" and a total. He has not decided anything yet.
drills.customerOpener: Okay. Honestly, this is way more detailed than what the other company sent me.
drills.techPrompt: Devin is comparing quotes. Ask what he wants to compare, go through the prices line by line, and respect his choice.
passCriteria: Ask what he wants to compare or learn from the other bids
Go through both quotes line by line and name the required items the lower one does not list
Do not cut the price, criticize the other company, or push for a decision
Offer your itemized estimate in writing and make it easy to come back

review.author: Claude
notes: second-opinion-quote also forces found-it-cheaper, and Devin holds it at 60 against 40 for need-three-bids. He raises the lower quote first, and three bids follows on a later turn. durationSec is 180 to fit both.
The opener only leads in and voices neither objection, so neither repeats.

drills.title: "Let me talk to my wife"
drills.why: This moment starts with "I need to talk to my wife first." Most techs treat it as a stall to get past. They ask, "Can't you just decide?" Or they offer a discount to sign before the spouse gets home. Others say, "No problem," and leave with nothing the customer can show anyone. Here's what is really going on. For many couples, it's not a stall. It's how they make decisions, and they're right to. The real worry is explaining it at home from memory, getting it wrong, and being blamed if it goes badly. So respect it right away. Offer to bring the spouse in now with a quick phone call. If that won't work, make it easy to explain later: a photo of what you found, the options and prices in writing, and your recommendation in one sentence they can repeat. Then set a specific time to talk to both of them. In this drill, Carlos wants to talk to Elena first. Help him include her.

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: Okay, here's the thing. I'm not deciding this without Elena. She's at work till five.

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: That makes sense. It's a big decision for both of you. Would she have two minutes for a quick call now?

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: Probably not. She's slammed at work. She doesn't really pick up.

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: Then I'll text you a photo of the leak and all three options with prices. The short version is that the fifty-gallon fixes the mornings without paying for tankless.

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: Okay. Yeah, that I can explain to her.

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: What time tonight works for me to call you both? I'll answer whatever she wants to ask.

drills.priorContext: The tech found that the 11-year-old 40-gallon tank is leaking at the base and is too small for a family of five, which is why the hot water runs out in the mornings. The tech presented three options, the same 40-gallon size for $1,890, a 50-gallon high-recovery tank for $2,850, and tankless for $5,450, and recommended the 50-gallon because it fixes the mornings for about half the price of tankless. Carlos asked good questions and understands the choices. Elena is at work until five. The tech just asked Carlos if he would like to go ahead.
drills.customerOpener: Okay, here's the thing. I'm not deciding this without Elena. She's at work till five.
drills.techPrompt: Carlos won't decide without Elena. Respect that, offer a way to include her now or later, and set a specific follow-up.
passCriteria: Respect the joint decision without pushing Carlos to decide alone
Offer to include Elena now by phone, or with photos and the options in writing
Give Carlos a one-sentence version of your recommendation he can repeat
Set a specific time to follow up with both of them

review.author: Claude
notes: The opener voices the stall. talk-to-my-spouse only fires on a decision ask, and Carlos holds brother-in-law-plumber (55) and too-expensive (50) above it (45), so an ask would bring one of those first. Timing objections never fire on their own, so the opener is not repeated.

startPhase is price, not close, on purpose. At close the engine treats the price as already heard, and the scenario's forced brother-in-law-plumber fires on the first turn. At price it stays quiet until the tech states a number. Recommend removing brother-in-law-plumber from tank-vs-tankless-family's forced list.
Elena can walk in as an ambient move (Carlos weights spouse-walks-in at 3). If she does, including her still passes.

drills.title: "Just do the cheap fix"
drills.why: This moment comes when the customer says, "Just do the cheapest thing." Most techs get it wrong in one of two ways. Some pitch the bigger option again, or tell a worst-case story to scare the customer off the basic one. Others agree to anything to keep the job, even skipping a code item to get the price down. Here's what is really going on. Choosing the cheapest option is a fair decision, and customers often have reasons they haven't told you. What they want to know is simple: will the cheap option actually work, or will I be paying again next year? So answer that question honestly. If the basic option is safe and does the job, say so, state the trade-off once, and respect the choice. If the shortcut they want isn't safe or isn't to code, say no plainly and give the reason. Then do the basic job well. In this drill, Rick wants the bare minimum. Tell him honestly what that is.

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: Look, what's the bare minimum to get them hot water today?

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: The standard one is the bare minimum. A leaking tank can't be repaired, so there's no cheaper fix that's safe.

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: What about the expansion tank? Skip it. My guy never puts those in.

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: I can't skip that one. This house has a pressure regulator, so code requires it, and without it the pressure climbs every time the water heats. Same with the straps and the permit.

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: Alright. So eighteen ninety is as low as it goes.

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: Yes, that's the lowest price for doing it safely. The other option mostly adds a longer warranty. I can have it in today.

drills.priorContext: Rick met the tech at his rental. The tech showed him that the 13-year-old 40-gallon gas tank is leaking from the bottom seam and that the old expansion tank is full of water and no longer works. The tech explained that the house has a pressure regulator, so a working expansion tank is required. The tech presented two options with prices, the standard 40-gallon with a 6-year warranty for $1,890 and a 10-year version for $2,490, both installed today from stock on the truck. The tenants have had no hot water since this morning.
drills.customerOpener: Alright. Two options. My tenant's been texting me every ten minutes.
drills.techPrompt: Ask Rick which option he wants. When he asks for the bare minimum, tell him honestly what is safe and what is required.
passCriteria: Say plainly that the standard option is the lowest-cost safe fix, and why
Name the required items (expansion tank, two straps, permit) and do not agree to skip them
State the trade-off once, without pushing the 10-year option or using scare talk
Respect his choice and offer the earliest install

review.author: Claude
notes: The tech's decision ask brings just-the-cheap-fix first. $1,890 is over Rick's $1,300 ceiling, so the engine voices his first price-group objection. If the tech does not ask, the scenario's forced handyman-can-do-it (55) fires first and the cheap fix follows.
In this scenario the cheapest option is already the recommended one, so the honest answer is that there is no cheaper safe fix. The test is refusing to skip the code items.

drills.title: "My brother-in-law is a plumber"
drills.why: This moment comes when the customer says, "My brother-in-law is a plumber." Most techs get defensive. Some question the relative's skill or license. Some list everything that could go wrong. Some drop the price to compete with family. All of it puts the customer in the position of defending someone they love. Here's what is really going on. Family loyalty is real, and the customer isn't trying to insult you. Often money is tight, and the relative is how they can afford the work. What they need to know is whether this is a job their relative can actually do. So speak well of the relative. Say plainly what this job takes: what you found, and what fixing it involves, like the permit and the equipment. Offer your camera video and written findings so the relative can see exactly what you saw. Keep your recommendation and your price. In this drill, Carlos says his brother-in-law Tony could do it. Help him compare fairly.

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: Honestly, my brother-in-law's a plumber. He could probably do this for a lot less.

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: That's great to have family in the trade. What kind of work does he do?

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: New construction, mostly. He's good, he's just busy.

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: Then he knows plumbing. This one means digging up about ten feet of old clay sewer pipe under the lawn and replacing it, with a permit and an inspection. I'll send you the camera video so Tony can see exactly what I saw.

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: Okay. Yeah, he'd want to see that first.

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: If he can take it on, great. If not, you have my estimate in writing. Just give me a call.

drills.priorContext: The Ruiz family's main sewer line backed up this morning. The tech cleared it with a root cutter, so the house drains again for now, then ran a camera and found roots growing into two joints of the old clay line about 40 feet out, under the front lawn near the ash tree. One of those joints is cracked and offset. The rest of the line is sound. Carlos watched the video with the tech. The tech presented three options, root clearing only for $495, a spot repair that replaces about 10 feet of the line for $5,400, and lining the whole line for $13,800, and recommended the spot repair. Carlos's sister's husband, Tony, does plumbing for a builder that puts up new houses.
drills.customerOpener: Okay. So it's roots, right where the ash tree is. I saw it on the screen.
drills.techPrompt: Carlos says his brother-in-law Tony could do it for less. Respect Tony, explain what the job takes, and offer the camera video.
passCriteria: Speak well of Tony without questioning his skill or license
Explain plainly what this repair involves, such as the digging, the permit, and the inspection
Offer the camera video and written findings so Tony can see the problem
Keep your recommendation and price without discounting to compete

review.author: Claude
notes: brother-in-law-plumber is Carlos's strongest objection, and drain-main-line-roots forces it too, so it fires on the first customer turn in objections. If the tech asks for a decision first, $5,400 is over Carlos's $1,500 ceiling, so too-expensive comes instead.

The priorContext and demo follow the scenario's findings and its spot-repair recommendation. The scenario says the house was built in 1968 and the persona says 1976, so the drill does not name a year.

drills.title: Financing as a monthly number
drills.why: This moment comes right after the price, when the total is more than the customer can pay at once. Most techs miss it in one of three ways. They never mention financing because they're afraid it sounds pushy. They say "We have financing" and move on, with no number. Or they push payments before they understand the problem. Here's what is going on for the customer. Most people won't say "I can't afford it." They say less than they mean, like "That's more than I have right now." They're embarrassed, and they're picturing the whole amount coming out of their savings at once. Eighteen ninety at once and forty-nine dollars a month can feel completely different to the same person. So first, thank them for telling you. Then give one specific monthly number for the option you recommended, and offer to show them the terms in writing. Then let them choose. In this drill, Margaret has just heard eighteen ninety. Listen for the worry.

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: Eighteen ninety. Well... I'd have to take that out of my savings, I suppose.

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: Thank you for telling me. A lot of people would rather leave their savings alone. Can I show you another way to do it?

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: Well, yes. I suppose that would be all right.

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: With financing, the standard option comes to forty-nine dollars a month. I'll show you the terms in writing, so you can see exactly what it costs over time.

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: Forty-nine a month. Oh, that I could manage.

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: Then it's your choice. Monthly, all at once, or take some time to think. Whatever feels right to you.

drills.priorContext: The tech showed Margaret the leak, explained that the 12-year-old tank cannot be repaired, presented three options, and recommended the standard 40-gallon gas heater. The tech then said the total for that option, $1,890, once and clearly. Margaret has been quiet for a few seconds. Financing has not been mentioned yet.
drills.customerOpener: Eighteen ninety. Well. Let me see.
drills.techPrompt: Margaret just heard $1,890. When she hints at a money worry, acknowledge it kindly, then offer the monthly number, $49.
passCriteria: Acknowledge her worry kindly before offering anything
Give a specific monthly number for the recommended option, $49 a month
Offer to show the terms in writing and leave the choice to her
Do not lower the price or push for a yes

review.author: Claude
notes: Starts in objections so the engine already has $1,890 heard, which is over Margaret's $1,800 ceiling. quiet-money-worry needs priceStated and priceAboveBudget in price or objections.

Margaret's own too-expensive (chance 0.8) is checked before forced behavior moves, so it may come first. Both lead to the same moment. A gentle question from the tech can bring her fixed-income reveal first instead.
The $49 comes from the scenario's standard option. Each company's financing terms replace it.

drills.title: The membership ask
drills.why: This is the moment you offer the membership. Most techs get it wrong in one of three ways. Some skip it because it feels like a sales pitch. Some read every benefit off a card. Some push it the same way, every time, to every customer. Here's what is going on for the customer. Many people have signed up for plans they never used or couldn't cancel, and they remember it. When they hear "membership," they want two answers. What does it do for my house? Is it worth the money? A long list answers neither. So offer it once, plainly, and connect it to today's visit. Name the two or three benefits that matter for this home. Put it in numbers: what it costs, and what it would have saved today. Say what it doesn't cover. Then let them decide, and accept a no. In this drill, Margaret's sink drains again. Offer the membership and answer her question.

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: It's draining fine now. Before I go, can I tell you about our maintenance plan? It takes a minute, and there's no pressure.

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: Well, all right. What would I actually get for it?

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: For your house, three things. Once a year we check the whole system, the water heater, the drains, and the shutoff valves. You get priority when something breaks, and a member discount on repairs.

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: And would it have saved me anything today?

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: A little, yes. I'll show you the exact amount on your bill. It doesn't pay for new equipment, though. Would you like it, or would you rather think it over?

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: Well, I'd like someone checking on things. Harold always did that.

drills.priorContext: Margaret's hall bathroom sink drained slowly for weeks and stopped completely last night. Before starting, the tech offered two options and she chose the basic clearing for $185. The tech cleaned the hair and soap out of the stopper and the trap, and a full basin now drains in a few seconds. The other drains in the house are fine. Margaret is not a member of any maintenance plan, and nobody has mentioned one to her yet.

drills.techPrompt: The sink is fixed. Offer the membership once, plainly. When Margaret asks what she gets, name what matters for her house.

Name two or three benefits that matter for her house, not the full list
Say what it would have saved her today and what it does not cover
Accept her answer without pushing

review.author: Claude
notes: Starts in wrapup so Margaret's too-expensive, which fires only in price, objections, and close, stays quiet. what-do-i-actually-get fires on the turn the tech offers the membership.
The demo names generic benefits (yearly check, priority, member discount). Company specs supply the real ones, the price, and the cancel terms.
Margaret brings up Harold herself in the last line. The tech should not use her late husband to sell the plan.
drain-simple-snake asks that the membership be mentioned once, as optional, and never tied to the repair. The pass criteria test exactly that. Its forced tests-your-honesty does not fire in wrapup.

drills.title: Asking for the decision
drills.why: This is the moment you ask the customer to decide. A lot of techs never actually ask. They finish explaining and stand there, or they say, "Let me know what you think," and start packing up. The customer is left to bring it up, and most won't. Other techs ask in a way that pushes, like "So we're good to go, right?" Or they ask three times in a row. Here's what the customer needs. Many are waiting for you to ask, because a clear question is easier to answer than a long silence. If you never ask, they wonder whether you believe your own recommendation. So recap first, in two or three sentences: what you found, what you recommend, and why it fits them. Then ask one clear question, and stop talking. Whatever they say tells you what to do next. Don't ask again unless something new has come up. In this drill, Margaret is out of questions. Recap and ask.

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: Well, I think that answers all my questions. You've been very patient with me.

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: I'm glad. So, to recap. Your tank is leaking and can't be repaired, and the standard heater fits how you live. It's eighteen ninety, everything included.

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: Yes. That all makes sense to me.

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: Would you like me to go ahead with the standard heater?

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: (pauses) Well... yes. I think that's the right thing. When could you do it?

drills.priorContext: The tech showed Margaret the leak, explained that the 12-year-old tank cannot be repaired, presented three options, and recommended the standard 40-gallon gas heater with a 6-year warranty. The tech said the total, $1,890, which includes the expansion tank, two seismic straps, the permit, and haul-away. Margaret asked what the expansion tank is for and how long the install takes, and the tech answered both. She has no more questions. The tech has not asked her to decide yet.
drills.customerOpener: Well, I think that answers all my questions. You've been very patient with me.
drills.techPrompt: Margaret has no more questions. Recap what you found and what you recommend, then ask her one clear question.
passCriteria: Recap the finding, your recommendation, and why it fits her in a few sentences
Ask one clear question she can answer yes or no
Stop talking after the question and let her answer
Respond to her answer without asking again or adding pressure

review.author: Claude
notes: At close the engine holds $1,890 against Margaret's $1,800 ceiling with no monthly number framed, so a first ask usually brings too-expensive. That tests the last criterion. The demo shows the yes a strong recap can earn once money is settled.

drills.title: Leaving well on a no
drills.why: This is the moment the customer says no, or not yet. Most techs do one of two things, and both cost them the job. Some push. They ask again, or they offer a price that's only good today. Others give up. They say, "Okay, no problem," and leave with nothing in writing and no plan. Here's what is really going on. "I need to think about it" usually means there's a question the customer hasn't asked yet, and often it's about money. How you treat them right now decides whether they ever call you back. So respect it right away. Ask once, gently, what they want to think through, and answer it if you can. If they still want time, leave the options in writing, offer to send them to anyone they want to show, and set a specific day and time to follow up. Make sure the home is safe until then. In this drill, Margaret wants to think it over. Leave well.

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: You've been very kind. But I suppose I'd like to think it over, if that's all right.

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: Of course it's all right. Can I ask what you'd like to think through? If I can answer it now, I'm happy to.

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: Oh, it's mostly the money. And I'd like to talk to my son Kevin first.

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: That makes sense. I'll leave all three options in writing, and I can email a copy to Kevin. Could I call you tomorrow at ten?

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: Tomorrow at ten would be fine. Thank you for not rushing me.

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: Of course. Before I go, I'll shut off the water to the tank so the leak doesn't get worse overnight.

drills.priorContext: The tech showed Margaret the leak, explained that the 12-year-old tank cannot be repaired, presented three options, and recommended the standard 40-gallon gas heater for $1,890. The tech answered her questions about what is included and then asked whether she would like to go ahead. Margaret is not ready to decide today.
drills.customerOpener: You've been very kind. But I suppose I'd like to think it over, if that's all right.
drills.techPrompt: Margaret wants to think it over. Ask once what she's weighing, then leave the options in writing and set a follow-up.
passCriteria: Accept the request without pushing, a deadline, or a today-only price
Ask once, gently, what she wants to think through
Leave the options in writing and set a specific day and time to follow up
Offer to shut off the water to the leaking tank before you leave

review.author: Claude
notes: The opener voices the stall. need-to-think-about-it only fires on a decision ask, and with $1,890 over her $1,800 ceiling the engine would voice too-expensive first. Because timing objections never fire on their own, the opener cannot be repeated. The move stays latent, so a second decision ask from the tech brings too-expensive.
A gentle question about what she is weighing usually brings her fixed-income reveal, which the tech can answer with the $49 monthly number before leaving.

drills.title: Correcting misplaced confidence
drills.why: This moment comes when a customer is confident about something that's wrong for their house. Usually it came from a video. Most techs handle it badly in one of two ways. Some make the customer feel foolish: "You can't believe everything on the internet." Others go along with it to avoid an argument, and the customer makes a big decision on bad information. Here's what is really going on. The customer did that research so they wouldn't get overcharged. Sounding confident is how they protect themselves when they don't know the trade. And most of what they found is partly right. So start with what they got right. Then correct the part that doesn't fit their house, in plain words, with a fact they can see or check, like the size of the gas line. Keep your honest recommendation. If they still want the other choice after hearing the facts, respect it. In this drill, Devin has watched videos about tankless. Correct him respectfully.

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: Basically every video I watched said tankless pays for itself in like two years.

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: They're right that tankless uses less gas. That part's real. For two people, though, the savings are small, so it takes a lot longer than two years to make back the extra cost.

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: Okay, but it runs on my existing gas line, right?

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: Good question. Not this one. Your line is half an inch, sized for a tank, and tankless needs a bigger line from the meter. I can show you.

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: Huh. None of the videos mentioned that part.

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: Most don't. I'd still recommend the tank for your house. But if you want tankless, I'll price it the right way, with everything it needs.

drills.priorContext: The tech found rust at the base and a slow seep on Devin's 11-year-old 50-gallon gas tank and explained that it is at the end of its life and should be replaced. Devin and his fiancée Nora have never run out of hot water with it. The tech also noticed that the gas line to the heater is 1/2 inch and that there is white scale on the fittings from hard water. Devin has watched several videos about tankless water heaters and is excited about them. The tech has not presented options yet.
drills.customerOpener: Okay, so it needs replacing. Honestly, I figured. I've been reading up on tankless.
drills.techPrompt: Devin repeats something he learned online. Say what he got right, correct the rest with facts about his house, and keep your recommendation.
passCriteria: Say what his claim gets right before you correct it
Correct the wrong part in plain words, with a fact about this house
Keep the honest recommendation without mocking the video or giving in
Treat tankless as a fair choice if he still wants it after the facts

review.author: Claude
notes: The scenario also forces watched-a-video, so the two lists merge into one move. It fires on the first customer turn in findings, because none of Devin's objections are due before options or price.
The demo gives no payback number, matching the scenario, which leaves payback unquantified on purpose.

drills.title: Re-engaging after a distraction
drills.why: This moment comes when the customer gets called away in the middle of your explanation. A phone call, a kid, someone at the door. Most techs handle the return badly. Some pick up mid-sentence as if nothing happened. Some sigh, or say, "As I was saying." Some start the whole explanation over at full length. Here's what is going on for the customer. When they come back, they've lost most of what you said, and they're still thinking about the call. They feel bad for making you wait. If you go on from where you stopped, they'll nod without following, and later they won't be able to explain it to anyone. So while they're away, stop and wait. When they come back, welcome them back warmly. Recap the main point in a sentence or two. Check that it still makes sense, then go on. In this drill, Jen's phone rings while you're explaining. Bring her back.

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: Sorry about that. Where were we?

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: No problem at all. Real quick, here's where we were. The camera showed the inside of the pipe is coated with grease, so snaking only opens a path through it, and it clogs again.

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: Oh, right. Okay. So that's why Dan's fix didn't hold.

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: Exactly. Does that part make sense? Any questions before I tell you how to clean it out so it stays clear?

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: No, that makes sense. Go ahead, I'm listening now.

drills.priorContext: Jen's kitchen sink backed up this morning, the third clog this year. Another company cleared it in the spring, and her husband Dan cleared it with a store-bought snake in the summer. Both times it came back within weeks. The tech opened the line with a cable so the sinks drain for now, then ran a camera down the kitchen drain and found why it keeps clogging, but has not explained it to Jen yet. Jen works from home, her two-year-old Theo is home today, and she is expecting a work call.
drills.customerOpener: Sorry, sorry. Okay, I'm here. What did the camera show?
drills.techPrompt: Explain what the camera showed. When Jen takes a call, wait. When she's back, recap in a sentence or two and check in.
passCriteria: Stop talking while she is on the phone
Welcome her back with no sign of impatience
Recap the main point in a sentence or two and check she is following
Go on without starting over at full length

review.author: Claude
notes: phone-call-hold-on fires on the first customer turn in findings, because none of Jen's objections are due before options or a decision ask. The runtime speaks the move's first followUp when she returns, which matches the first demo line.
drain-kitchen-recurring also forces just-the-cheap-fix. It needs a stated price and options, so it stays quiet unless the tech gets to the $265 and $625 options in this drill.
The priorContext follows the scenario's history (one clearing by another company, one by Dan with a store-bought snake). Jen's persona fact says Dan tried twice. Align the two.

drills.title: Bringing in the second decision-maker
drills.why: This moment happens when the other decision-maker walks in partway through. Most techs make one of three mistakes. They nod at the new person and keep talking to the first one. They start over and repeat everything at full length. Or they ask for a decision before the new person knows what's going on. Here's what is really happening. The person who just walked in often has an equal say, and they heard none of your explanation. If they aren't caught up, the answer at the end will be, "We need to talk about it." They also notice right away whether you're talking to them or only to their partner. So stop and greet them by name. Give a short recap in plain words: what you found, the options, and what you recommend and why. Keep it to three or four sentences. Then ask what matters to them. In this drill, you're going over options with Carlos when Elena walks in. Catch her up.

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: Hi, sorry, I was getting the kids out the door. What did you find?

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: Hi, you must be Elena. I'm Chris. Here's the short version. Your tank is leaking and has to be replaced, and it's too small for five people. That's why you run out in the mornings.

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: Okay. That explains a lot. Mornings are a nightmare around here.

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: There are three ways to fix it, and I'm recommending the fifty-gallon. It stops the running out for about half the cost of tankless. What matters most to you in this?

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: Honestly? I just want it fixed once, so we're not doing this again.

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: That's fair. Let me show you both how long each option should last.

drills.priorContext: The tech found that the 11-year-old 40-gallon tank is leaking at the base and cannot be repaired, and that 40 gallons is too small for a family of five, which is why the hot water runs out in the mornings. The tech showed Carlos the leak in the garage and is now going over three options with him, the same 40-gallon size, a 50-gallon high-recovery tank, and tankless. No prices have been given yet. Elena has been inside getting the kids out the door and has heard none of this.
drills.customerOpener: Okay. So the fifty-gallon one, that's enough for all five of us?
drills.techPrompt: When Elena walks in, stop. Greet her, catch her up in a few sentences, and ask what matters to her.
passCriteria: Stop and greet Elena by name when she walks in
Recap what you found and the options in three or four plain sentences
Ask what matters to her or what questions she has
Do not ask for a decision before she is caught up

review.author: Claude
notes: spouse-walks-in fires on the first customer turn. In options none of Carlos's objections are due yet, because they all need a stated price or a decision ask.

tank-vs-tankless-family also forces brother-in-law-plumber. It stays quiet until the tech states a price, then fires on the next turn. That is realistic, since Elena is tired of Tony's fixes, but it pulls focus. Recommend removing it from the scenario's forced list.

drills.title: "Would you do this in your own house?"
drills.why: At some point a customer will ask, "Would you do this in your own house?" Most techs miss it. Some dodge with "It's totally up to you." Some name the most expensive option with no reason. Some make up a story about their own house. Customers can tell. Here's what the question really means. The customer is asking whether they can trust you. Many have been sold work they didn't need. They want a real answer, not a pitch. A straight answer with a reason that fits their house often decides whether they hire you, even when it's the cheaper option. So answer it directly. Say what you would actually do, and why, using what you found and what they told you. If the honest answer is the cheaper option, say so. Then tell them what would change your answer. Don't follow it with a push to get started. In this drill, Tasha asks what you'd do. Tell her the truth.

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: Okay. Be honest with me. If this was your house, what would you do?

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: I'd do the repair. Your tank isn't leaking and there's no rust. The part that failed is small, and replacing it fixes the problem.

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: So you wouldn't replace it? It's nine years old.

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: Not today. Tanks around here usually last eight to twelve years. I'd fix this and start setting money aside for a new one. If it ever starts leaking, that's when you replace it.

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: Huh. The last guy would've sold me the whole tank.

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: I'll put both options in writing, so you can look them over after you've slept.

drills.priorContext: Tasha just got home from a night shift. The tech tested the thermocouple with a meter, showed her the low reading, and explained that it is why the pilot keeps going out. The tank itself is sound, with no leaks or rust. The tech presented two options, replacing the thermocouple and cleaning the air intake screen for $325, or replacing the whole 9-year-old tank for $1,890, and said the repair is the honest fix.
drills.customerOpener: Okay. So you're saying I don't need a new one. Just this part.
drills.techPrompt: Tasha asks what you would do in your own house. Give a direct, honest answer with a reason that fits her.
passCriteria: Answer the question directly with what you would actually do
Give a reason based on this tank and what she told you
Recommend the repair, and say when replacement would make sense
Do not follow the answer with a push to decide

review.author: Claude
notes: would-you-do-this fires on the first customer turn unless her how-do-i-know-its-broken (chance 0.6) comes first. That only happens while her trust is under 55, so a first answer that shows the reading usually brings the probe right away.
The scenario also forces tests-your-honesty. It follows on a later turn with a related probe, such as whether she could get another year out of it.

drills.title: Catching and using a dropped detail
drills.why: This moment is easy to miss. While you're working, the customer mentions something in passing. A pet. A grown kid who lives out of town. A trip coming up. Most techs nod and keep going, and twenty minutes later they give the same presentation they give everyone. Here's why those details matter. They're what the customer actually cares about, and most people won't say them twice. When you bring one back later, the customer knows you were listening to them, not just looking at the equipment. That does more for trust than anything you can say about yourself. So when a customer mentions a person, a pet, a plan, or a worry, respond briefly and remember it. Then use it later where it fits: in how you work, in a question, or in your recommendation. Keep the door closed so the cat stays in. Offer to send the options to the son. In this drill, Margaret will mention two things in passing. Catch one and use it.

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: Before I look at the heater, tell me a little about the house. Who lives here with you?

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: Oh, just me and Biscuit, my cat. She's hiding somewhere. She doesn't like strangers.

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: I'll keep an eye out for her. Does anyone help you with house things like this?

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: My son Kevin, when he can. But he's up in Bakersfield, and I hate to bother him.

demo.speaker: tech
demo.text: Then when I write up your options, I can email a copy to Kevin so he can look it over. And I'll keep the garage door shut so Biscuit can't get out.

demo.speaker: customer
demo.text: Oh, would you? That's very thoughtful of you. Thank you.

drills.priorContext: The tech has just introduced themselves at the front door and explained how the visit will go. Margaret is leading the tech through the house toward the garage. Her gray cat, Biscuit, slipped out of the bedroom when the doorbell rang and is hiding somewhere nearby. This morning Margaret mentioned the hot water problem to her son Kevin on the phone. He lives two hours away in Bakersfield, and she does not like to bother him with house problems.
drills.techPrompt: Ask about Margaret and her home. When she mentions something personal, remember it and use it before the drill ends.
passCriteria: Ask at least two open questions about Margaret, not only the heater
Respond briefly when she mentions Biscuit or Kevin
Later, use one of those details in how you work, a question, or a recommendation

review.author: Claude
notes: No customerOpener, so the tech speaks first. The persona reveals Biscuit after the first tech turn and Kevin on household or budget topics.
The priorContext puts both details in front of the customer model, so they come up even if the tech asks few questions.

companies.name: Summit Plumbing & Air
companies.about: Summit Plumbing & Air is a family-owned plumbing and HVAC company founded in 2008. It serves homeowners across Riverside County. Its techs give every customer options and a written, flat-rate price before any work starts. Its Summit Care Club membership covers a yearly water heater flush, priority scheduling, and member pricing on repairs.
brandVoice: Friendly and calm. Sound like a helpful neighbor who knows plumbing, not like a salesperson.
Plain and specific. Use plain words and real numbers, and explain any trade term you use.
Options, not pressure. Lay out the choices, give your recommendation and the reason, and let the customer decide.
Accountable. Put it in writing, do what you said you would do, and own it if something goes wrong.

promises.label: Written, flat-rate price before work starts
promises.detail: Every job gets a written, flat-rate price before any work begins. The price does not change unless the customer approves a change in writing.

promises.label: Options on every job
promises.detail: Every customer sees their options, including the simplest fix that will hold, with the tech's recommendation and the reason for it.

promises.label: Respect for the home
promises.detail: Shoe covers at the door, drop cloths under the work area, and a clean work area before the tech leaves. Old parts and packaging leave with the tech.

promises.label: Two-hour arrival window
promises.detail: Customers get a two-hour arrival window and a call or text when the tech is on the way.

promises.label: 2-year labor warranty
promises.detail: Repairs and installations carry a 2-year labor warranty. Equipment and parts carry the manufacturer's warranty.

promises.label: 24/7 emergency service
promises.detail: Emergency service is available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.

process.name: Arrive and set the frame
process.description: Arrive inside the two-hour window. Put on shoe covers at the door. Introduce yourself and Summit, and confirm the customer's name and why they called. Lay out the plan: a few questions, an inspection, a look at what you find, and options with a written price. The customer decides, with no pressure.

process.name: Ask before you diagnose
process.description: Ask what they have noticed, when it started, what has been done before, how old the system is, who lives in the home, how long they plan to stay, and what matters most to them: cost, timing, or doing it once. Write down what they say.

process.name: Inspect
process.description: Put drop cloths under the work area. Diagnose the problem they called about, then check the related items a careful tech would check. On a water heater, that means the venting, the gas or electrical connection, the seismic straps, the expansion tank, and the water pressure. Take photos of what you find.

process.name: Show and explain what you found
process.description: Show the photos or the part. Explain each finding in plain words: what it is, why it matters, and how urgent it is. Say what is in good shape too. Do not recommend work the findings do not support.

process.name: Present options
process.description: Give two or three options tied to what the customer told you, including the simplest fix that will hold. Say which one you recommend for their home and why, in one or two sentences.

process.name: Give the written price
process.description: Write a flat-rate price for each option before any work begins. Say the price clearly, once, then stop talking and let the customer think.

process.name: Answer questions honestly
process.description: Ask what questions they have and answer each concern directly. When cost is the concern, show what is included, go back to the other options, and explain financing as a monthly number with its real terms. Never use pressure or urgency that is not real.

process.name: Ask for the decision
process.description: Ask plainly which option they want, and get their signature on the written price. If the scope changes mid-job, stop and get their approval in writing before you go further.

process.name: Offer the Summit Care Club
process.description: If they are not a member, offer the Summit Care Club once and tie it to what you found. It is $19.95 a month, month to month: a yearly water heater flush, priority scheduling, 15 percent off repairs, and no overtime fees. Accept a no without a second push.

process.name: Clean up and leave well
process.description: Clean the work area and take old parts and packaging with you. Test the work with the customer and show them what you did. Explain the 2-year labor warranty and thank them. On a no, leave the written options with them and thank them just the same.

preferred.line: Hi, I'm [your name] with Summit Plumbing and Air. Thanks for having me out. Let me put my shoe covers on before I come in.
Here's my plan. I'll ask a few questions, take a look, and show you what I find. Then I'll give you a few options with prices in writing, and you decide. No pressure either way.
Tell me what's been going on. When did you first notice it?
Let me show you what I found. Here's the problem, here's why it matters, and here's what looks fine.
I've got three options for you. Here's what each one includes, and here's the one I'd pick for your house, and why.
Here's the price in writing. It's flat rate, so it won't change once I start unless you approve a change.
If it's easier to spread out, there's zero percent for twelve months, or a sixty-month plan with a smaller monthly payment. Want me to show you both?

One more thing, and it's totally optional. The Summit Care Club is nineteen ninety-five a month. You get a yearly water heater flush, priority scheduling, fifteen percent off repairs, and no overtime fees. Want to hear more?
Which of these feels right to you?
No problem at all. Here's everything in writing so you can think it over. If you have questions, call me.

I need an answer before I leave.
Trust me.

objectionAnswers.answer: Of course. Every option and its price goes in writing before I start. It's flat rate, so the number on the paper is the number you pay. If I find something else once I'm in there, I stop and get your okay in writing before I do anything more.

That makes sense. Can I ask what you'll be comparing, price or what's included? I'll put every option in writing, line by line, so it's easy to compare. If you have questions about the other quotes, call me and I'll tell you straight.

I hear you. Let me show you what's in that number. If one of the other options fits your budget better, we can go that way. And if spreading it out would help, there's zero percent for twelve months, or a sixty-month plan with a smaller monthly payment.

companies.name: Gardner Plumbing Co.
companies.about: Gardner Plumbing Co. is a family-owned company based in Murrieta that has served Riverside County since 1995. It works in homes, HOAs, restaurants, and small to mid-size commercial properties. The business started as Nootbar Plumbing. The Gardner family took ownership in 2020 and renamed it Gardner Plumbing Co. in 2024. It offers plumbing, HVAC, and electrical service. The company calls its promise on every call The Gardner Standard: written estimates, no trip fees, clean visits, and a 30-day guarantee.
brandVoice: Warm and respectful. The company describes its approach as treating every customer like a valued neighbor. Use the customer's name and take care with their home and their time.
Plain and direct. Short sentences, plain words, and real numbers. Explain any trade term you use.
Confident without pushing. State the recommendation and the price once, clearly, then let the customer think.

Accountable. The company's own line is "We own it." Point to the written estimate and the 30-day guarantee instead of making verbal promises. If something goes wrong, say so and say what you will do about it.
No pressure. A no, a wait, or a second opinion is fine, and the customer should hear that from you.

promises.label: 30-Day Callback Guarantee
promises.detail: If the same issue comes back within 30 days of the visit, a technician returns at no charge. Parts from the original job are re-supplied at no cost, and callback labor is covered with no trip fee or hourly rate. It covers the same root cause, not a separate problem somewhere else.

promises.label: Written Estimate Before Work Begins
promises.detail: Every job starts with a written estimate listing scope, materials, and labor. The number you sign is the number you pay. If the scope changes mid-job, work stops and a revised estimate is presented, and nothing goes further without the customer's written sign-off.

promises.label: No Trip Fees, No Pressure
promises.detail: Free in-home estimate with zero obligation. No dispatch fee, service-call fee, or fuel surcharge. A customer who declines the estimate owes nothing. The company says it never uses pressure tactics or inflated book-rate pricing to create urgency.

promises.label: Clean Visit Promise
promises.detail: Six steps on every call: shoe covers before stepping inside, drop cloths under every work area, path protection from the entry to the work area, towels around every fixture, full cleanup before the job is called done, and haul-away of all old parts and packaging. If a step is missed, a technician comes back the same business day at no charge.

promises.label: 1-Year Workmanship Guarantee
promises.detail: Installations and repairs carry a 1-year workmanship guarantee. Parts carry the manufacturer's warranty. Warranty details are written on the invoice.

promises.label: Fully Licensed, Bonded and Insured
promises.detail: CSLB license number 1073177, which customers can look up at cslb.ca.gov. The company carries liability insurance and workers' compensation.

process.name: Arrive, protect the home, and set the frame
process.description: Put shoe covers on at the door, before stepping inside. This is the first step of the Clean Visit Promise. Introduce yourself and Gardner Plumbing, and confirm the customer's name and why they called. Explain the visit: you will look, show them what you find, and give them a written estimate before any work begins. Say there is no trip fee and no obligation to go ahead.

process.name: Ask before you diagnose
process.description: Ask what they have noticed, when it started, what has been done before, how old the system is, how long they plan to stay in the home, and what matters most to them: cost, timing, or doing it once. Listen and write down what they say. Their answers shape the options.

process.name: Inspect and protect the work area
process.description: Follow the Clean Visit Promise before any tool comes out: path protection from the entry to the work area, a drop cloth under the work area, and clean towels around every fixture. Diagnose the problem they called about, then check the related items a careful plumber would check. Take photos or camera video of what you find.

process.name: Show and explain what you found
process.description: Show the photos, the camera video, or the part itself. Explain each finding in plain words: what it is, why it matters, and how urgent it is. Say what is in good shape too. Do not recommend work the findings do not support.

process.name: Present options
process.description: Give two or three options tied to what the customer told you, including the simplest repair that will hold when there is one. Say which option you recommend for their home and why, in one or two sentences.

process.name: Written estimate before work begins
process.description: Write the estimate before any work begins: scope, materials, and labor, with permit fees on their own line. Pricing is flat rate, so the price does not change with the clock. Say the price clearly, once, then stop talking and let the customer think. The number they sign is the number they pay.

process.name: Answer questions honestly
process.description: Ask what questions they have and answer each concern directly. When cost is the concern, show what is in the price, offer the other options, and explain financing as a monthly number with its real terms. A second opinion is fine, and the estimate visit costs them nothing. Never use pressure or urgency that is not real.

process.name: Ask for the decision
process.description: Ask plainly which option they would like to go with. Get their written sign-off on the estimate before starting. If the scope changes mid-job, stop, write a revised estimate, and do not continue without their written sign-off.

process.name: Offer The Gardner Shield
process.description: If they are not a member, offer The Gardner Shield once and tie it to what you found. Bronze (plumbing) is $249 a year: two plumbing maintenance visits, 10 percent off plumbing services, one free drain cleaning a year with an accessible cleanout, priority dispatch, and no emergency overtime charges. Silver adds HVAC for $348 a year, and Gold adds HVAC and electrical for $397 a year. Say clearly that it is not a warranty. Accept a no without a second push.

process.name: Clean up, explain the guarantee, and leave well
process.description: Finish the Clean Visit Promise: sweep or vacuum the work area, wipe down surfaces you touched, and remove all debris. Old parts and packaging leave on the Gardner truck unless the customer asks to keep them. Walk the customer through the work, explain the 30-day callback guarantee and the warranty terms on the invoice, and thank them. On a no, leave the written estimate and thank them just the same.

membership.name: The Gardner Shield
membership.summary: Annual membership in three tiers. Bronze Shield (plumbing) is $249 a year, Silver Shield (plumbing and HVAC) is $348 a year, and Gold Shield (plumbing, HVAC, and electrical) is $397 a year. A plumbing and electrical combination is $298 a year. The company states it is not a warranty plan. It is a direct relationship with a licensed contractor: scheduled maintenance, priority service, no emergency overtime, and member discounts.
benefits: Two plumbing maintenance visits a year

One free drain cleaning a year with an accessible cleanout

Silver Shield adds two HVAC tune-ups a year (spring AC and fall heating), a refrigerant level check at every tune-up, 10 percent off HVAC services, and priority scheduling during summer AC failures.
Gold Shield adds an annual electrical safety inspection with a whole-home electrical safety report, 10 percent off electrical services, and priority response after storms and outages.

Interest is billed during the promo period and waived only if the amount financed is paid in full by the end, and minimum payments alone will not pay it off in time. GreenSky Plan 1519 is 11.99 percent APR fixed for 180 months, about $119.95 a month for every $10,000 financed (the site calls this an estimate). It's a flat price, so it doesn't change if the job takes longer. You're also getting a labor warranty that runs about twice as long as most companies', and a van that's stocked to finish the job today.

Sometimes it can, so here's my honest read on yours. If it's still working and not leaking, waiting is a real option, and I'll tell you what to watch for. If the tank itself is leaking, that won't get better, and I'd plan for it soon. Either way, the written price is yours to keep, and we're here 24/7 if it gets worse.

If a repair makes sense, that's what I'll recommend. We'll always tell you when a repair is the better value. If the part that failed can be fixed and the tank is sound, the repair is the right call. If the tank itself is failing, a repair won't hold, and I'll show you why.

Yes, and here's why. California code requires seismic straps and a thermal expansion tank when a water heater goes in, and the permit is part of doing it to code. That's why they're already in your written price instead of added on later.

Fair. We don't do the "while I'm here" add-ons. I'll show you what I found, tell you honestly if a repair makes more sense than replacing, and you choose. You can walk away anytime.

facts: Founded in 2019 by owner Anna M. Family-owned and locally operated, based in Lake Elsinore.
California contractor license number 1140776. Licensed, bonded, and insured.
Water heater specialists. Gas, electric, tankless, and heat pump water heaters, repaired or replaced across the Inland Empire. Also plumbing and HVAC.
Same-day service. Fully stocked vans are ready to finish the job on the first visit.
24/7 emergency service.
SOS says its labor warranty is, on average, about twice as long as most competitors'.
Upfront, written, flat-rate pricing. The written number is the number the customer pays, and a scope change means the tech stops and re-quotes first.
Water heater estimates include the code upgrades California requires (seismic strapping, a thermal expansion tank, and T&P valve discharge routing) and the permit fee.
Water heater brands shown on the site: Rheem, Rinnai, Bradford White, and Navien.
Financing is available for larger repairs and replacements.

review.author: Claude
notes: Written from waterheatersos.com pages retrieved 2026-10-22. All listed pages loaded. FAQ answers on the site are collapsed and did not appear in the page text, so nothing from them is used.

Verify with the owner. Labor warranty length. The home page says "Our labor warranty, on average, is twice as long than most of our competitors," but no page states the length in years. Scripts say "about twice as long" and promise the exact terms in writing. Add the real length once confirmed.

Verify with the owner. Fees. The site says quotes are free with no obligation, but /transparent-pricing lists a $49 to $89 service call or dispatch fee (applied toward the repair when the work is approved on the same visit) and an $89 to $149 diagnostic fee ("waived or applied"). Confirm when each fee applies, whether either applies to a free replacement estimate, and what a customer owes if they decline. The spec tells techs to disclose any fee before it applies.
Verify with the owner. The site shows a "No OT Fees" badge and also lists a $149 to $249 after-hours or emergency fee. Confirm what "No OT Fees" means. The spec does not use it in scripts or facts.

Verify with the owner. Financing. The site says only "Flexible payment options for larger repairs and replacements, ask your technician." Lender, rates, terms, minimums, and credit requirements are not stated, so financing is verified: false and no terms appear in scripts.

Verify with the owner. Membership. No membership or maintenance plan appears on the site, so there is no membership block. The process step recommends the yearly flush the site describes and is marked required: false. If SOS has a membership, add it here.

Verify with the owner. Brands. The site shows Rheem, Rinnai, Bradford White, and Navien logos as trusted water heater brands, along with Hajoca, which is a supply house. Confirm which brands SOS installs and stocks on the vans.
Verify with the owner. Haul-away of the old water heater is not mentioned on the site, so the spec does not promise it.

Verify with the owner. Base location. The About page says "a family-owned business based in Redlands, California," but every page lists 571 Crane St, Unit H, Lake Elsinore. The spec uses Lake Elsinore.
Verify with the owner. Ratings. The home page shows 4.9 from 542 Google reviews, other pages show 5.0 with no source, and one counter reads "0+ Reviews." Ratings are left out of facts.
Verify with the owner. A "Satisfaction Guarantee" badge appears with no terms, so it is not used as a promise.

Verify with the owner. The home page mentions heat pump water heater rebates under California and IRA programs. Federal incentive rules have changed since the IRA passed, so confirm which programs are current before techs cite any rebate.

Verify with the owner. /discount-water-heaters lists booking offers ($100 off a water heater replacement, $250 off a tankless installation, $25 off a flush, and $300 off whole-house water filtration) with "mention code at time of booking." No code, expiration, or stacking rules are shown. Not used in scripts. Confirm whether techs can honor them in the home.

Verify with the owner. The site shows "CA LIC# 1140776" without naming the license classifications. Confirm the classifications for plumbing and HVAC work, and how techs should refer to the owner (the About page lists "Anna M.").
The process steps, brand voice, scripts, and objection answers were written by Claude from the site's promises. The owner should confirm they match how SOS trains its techs.
